title: As ‘Hello Kitty’ Joins Thanksgiving Parade, Sanrio Execs Tease ‘Magical’ Warner Bros. Animated Movie, Video Game Plans and 50-Year-Old Brand’s Gen Alpha Strategy
full_text: × Nov 25, 2026 11:00am PT As ‘Hello Kitty’ Joins Thanksgiving Parade, Sanrio Execs Tease ‘Magical’ Warner Bros. Animated Movie, Video Game Plans and 50-Year-Old Brand’s Gen Alpha Strategy By Jennifer Maas Plus Icon Jennifer Maas TV Business Writer @jmaasaronson Latest Dropout’s ‘Very Important People’ Reveals Season 4 Release Date; Adds Ben Schwartz, Kirby Howell-Baptiste and More Guests 30 minutes ago ‘GTA 6’ Has At Least 9 Distinct Endings 3 hours ago ‘Metal Slug’ Live-Action Movie Set From ‘I Love My Dad’ Writer James Morosini, The Arena (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Sanrio/Macy's For those uninitiated into the Sanrio community, the beloved character Hello Kitty is a little girl (yes, girl) who is five apples tall. On Thursday, she’ll reach 107 apples tall when she takes flight (New York City weather permitting) as a balloon in Macy’s 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade. While a huge culture moment for Sanrio’s Hello Kitty and Friends brand, it’s far from the only major move the Japanese-based lifestyle and entertainment brand has been making around the world this year to connect with a wide range of age demographics and pockets of culture. Related Stories Brad Pitt Says 'Ocean's 14' Not Shooting Until 'Late' 2027 Oscars Visual Effects Top 20 Revealed: Disney Leads With Four Titles as ‘The Odyssey,’ ‘Ramayana,’ ‘Dune: Part Three’ and ‘Wildwood’ Make the Cut (EXCLUSIVE) And it’s been working: Sanrio achieved record results for the end of its fiscal year March 2026, reporting a 33.9% increase in sales year over year. Created in 1974 by Japanese designer Yuko Shimizu as a cute character for Sanrio products, Hello Kitty has become a global brand that partners with major sporting leagues including the F1, MLB, NHL, NFL and top musicians like Bruno Mars and Katseye. Along with all those tie-in products across everything from fashion to kitchenware and even several Hello Kitty-themed cafes throughout North America, there is a huge transmedia strategy in play at Sanrio, including multiple Hello Kitty video games (“Island Adventure” and the newly released “Party Land”), comic books, a digital series on YouTube and even a Hello Kitty animated movie made in collaboration with Warner Bros Pictures that’s set to release in theaters in July 2028. (The English-language feature project was first announced by New Line in 2019 and was dated last October after several years in development.) See below for Variety ‘s Q&A with Sanrio’s Craig Takiguchi, Chief Executive Office for the U.S. and the Americas and Jill Koch, Chief Brand Officer for U.S. and the Americas. When it comes to focusing on different age groups, being a family-friendly brand across ages, how do you look at the next generation and balancing those consumers with the existing Sanrio community? Craig Takiguchi: In the simplest of terms, there’s a lot of influences in our audiences’ lives, our communities’ lives. Fundamentally, we’re for ages six to 11 and 18 to 34. And 18-34 is kind of this flywheel where they have families of their own or they have extended families, and they introduce the brand to a whole new generation. On the other hand, Gen Z and Gen Alpha, we believe, are fundamentally different from any other brand previously and that is they are digital natives. When I grew up, my biggest influences were theatrical and maybe cartoon. Theirs are content on YouTube and gaming, and so subsequently, we go to where they already are. We think disproportionately gaming will be a big influence in the next five to 10 years. Because when we extrapolate the kids today and what they’re doing with their time, maybe you go to a movie and you see it twice, maybe three times. You watch a TV series, you can see it several times. But when you play games, they’re playing hundreds of times. So when they become captains of industry or ways to make decisions for a broader community, they’re going to look at their influences and so that is the reason why we’re in content, gaming, live experiences. Experiences are a big part of our brand, and fundamentally, because we believe that you cannot replace that energy of fandom outside of real life. And that’s what brings people literally and figuratively together in a way that allows them to wear their favorite outfit or their favorite character and represent as part of something bigger than themselves. Why is now finally the time for a “Hello Kitty” movie when the character and brand have been growing and building since the 70s? I know the project has been in development for some time — what affected that process? Takiguchi: We’ve found unique ways to capture the imagination of communities in the market. We always try to be authentic in that way, so we don’t necessarily follow the convention, especially in North America, where we’re not predominantly a North American brand and our value is a little different from the North American thesis. I think it’s a combination of a lot of things. We would have probably preferred to bring it out earlier too if we had the ability. But building this flywheel to the market was very important for us. It is not just a movie moment, and we also know that there was a confluence of events that made theatrical release not as attractive. So timing of the market was also very important. The other part that was important was on our side, which is we had to get the right team and it is a unique brand. It’s not built for everybody, and the storytelling mechanic was super, super important to us. So I’m not saying we had the wrong team in place before, but we went through a lot of different adjustments, both on our side and where we were going to launch in the market to make sure the timing was right. Like all things, in life it was meant to be. I think 2028 release, we couldn’t have picked a better position. We couldn’t have picked a better partner to do it. And everyone that is around the movie, I think, has some kind of tear-jerking moment, because the story, which we will reveal to the rest of the world, is so timely and it’s also something genuine. It’s got this magical transformation that we think will be unique to our brand, but also be universally appealing. Jill Koch: When Hello Kitty was created back in the 1970s, it was created for products, so we didn’t have content, entertainment, any of that back then. So I think, as Craig was talking about content and gaming and our journey there, as we have grown into a lifestyle and entertainment brand, it’s part of the story. So we’ve done these other things, and this is like a natural progression. So timing is right from that perspective, too. What else can you say about the plot of the animated film and whether it will be in a meta context, like the “Barbie” movie? Takiguchi: Even though theatrical moments are literally just that, it’s a movie moment, I think it is a magical transformation that everybody can relate to. So it’s universally appealing, and it’s something that goes to the heart I think of maybe why we’re all here and how it’s the basis of all our friendships, all our loving relationships, that in a crazy world of you know pandemics and geopolitical concerns and technological obsolescence and human obsolescence, if you will. I think it brings us all back to humans and empowers us in a magical way that can impact everybody’s lives. That’s the best I can give you at this moment in time. And Hello Kitty is a human. I’m still trying to tell people Sanrio has confirmed she’s a little girl. Takiguchi: There’s a haunting sort of mystery around the character. How are you approaching global expansion? Takiguchi: I would say, as we represent North America because we’re a global brand and how we go to market in Japan, where we represent a huge market share, is very different from how we would really find relevance with communities here. Because we’re not that big, we’re a market taker, so we cannot set the global trend around it. It’s just too expensive, and it’s not us, too. We’re kind of more of an intimate brand. So one of the things we see with you smartphone, for example, there’s a lot of convergence in all forms of technology and it’s bringing these communities closer and closer together. So when we look at our tangential audiences, we see sports, we see music, we see all forms of entertainment and so bringing them together whether it’s a collaboration, whether it’s a pop-up, whether it’s in-event activity, it seems to be where the audience is. And I hope it’s not a form of convenience where it’s like a convenience store; you can go to one place and pick up all your fandom. But it gives us a little bit of a license to play in the sports arena and tap into those communities where we never had access to before. What have you seen so far in the reaction to the live experiences, like the sporting events and cafes? Koch: We find too, like with all events, but sports in particular, our fans crave interacting together and going to an event together. With all the games, in a lot of cases, a lot of girlfriends will get together and that might be the one baseball game they go to all year, where eight of them will go together and it’ll be like their special day out or family or dad and daughter. So we also see from a fan perspective, they love that and they also love meeting other fans that obviously share the love of the brand. I’ll use this last Dodgers game as a good example from August. We had a blind box plush as the game giveaway, so it was one of five [possible Hello Kitty and Friends characters in the box], and we saw with fans all the content they posted after. So many were opening it, and like, “Oh, I love Pompompurin, but I wanted Kuromi” and then meeting a stranger and exchanging and making new friends. So for us, that was everything. It’s like coming together, making new friends, sharing a connection, which is what people love about our brand. And that emotional connection is what makes our brand unique. So to see that all come together at once is really fulfilling from the brand side of things. title: Ariana Grande Says ‘Petal’ Music Video Backlash Felt Like ‘Black Mirror’ and ‘I Wouldn’t Change a Thing. I’d Put It Out Again Today As Is’
full_text: × Nov 25, 2026 10:55am PT Ariana Grande Says ‘Petal’ Music Video Backlash Felt Like ‘Black Mirror’ and ‘I Wouldn’t Change a Thing. I’d Put It Out Again Today As Is’ By Steven J. Horowitz Plus Icon Steven J. Horowitz Senior Music Writer speriod Latest Ariana Grande’s ‘Eternal Sunshine Tour’ Concert Movie and Making-of Documentary to Stream on Peacock in December 1 day ago U2 Announces North American Leg of ‘Greatest Show on Earth’ Global Stadium Tour for 2027 1 day ago ‘Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album’ Deluxe Adds 23 Original Songs From Travis Scott, Slayyyter, Offset, Sexyy Red and More 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images Ariana Grande has spoken out about the criticism she received for her “Petal” music video, describing it as an episode of “Black Mirror” but caveating that she “wouldn’t change a thing” and “would put it out again today as is.” The pop star made the comments during an appearance on Las Culturistas podcast while discussing her latest album “Petal” and the visuals for the title track. In the video, which was released in August, Grande plays a character named Pepper who faces criticism from a panel of male judges as she auditions for a role, changing who she is to appease them. In the end, she snaps, brandishing a chainsaw in a murderous rampage as she realizes she doesn’t need to conform to someone else’s perception of her. Related Stories 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Spins Up Massive Numbers for Sony's Quarterly Earnings Jo Koy on ‘Blue in the Face,’ Steven Spielberg, Biggie’s Mom and Learning What His Name Really Means at Long John Silver’s Grande addressed the backlash to the video that, ironically, focused on her appearance instead of the message. “It’s kind of like, when will it be about the art? When will it be about the work? That was largely what the video was about,” she said. “It’s like, oh here comes this girl. And there’s always some distortion around the performance or art, whatever it is.” Subsequently, she said, “[It] had its own meta insane perception, and that was really interesting. But I feel so proud and grateful, I wouldn’t change a thing. I would put it out again today as is, I wouldn’t change a thing. I think my experience of putting art out and having people receive it is so different than how it used to be even just a few years ago.” Following the video’s criticism, Grande released a statement declaring that she would be taking a “step back from visibility” after her “Eternal Sunshine” tour. In hindsight, she says, the backlash was something akin to an episode of “Black Mirror.” “I really thought it was going to be a reveal, like me sharing a vulnerable… Like OK, here’s this thing and then it happened sometimes 10 back,” she said. “It was very funny and weird, but like I said, I love that project, I love that video. Those are two of my favorite videos, ‘Hate That I Made You Love Me’ and ‘Petal.’ I remember how it felt to be in the room, too, with all of those women dancers and all of us discussing what it felt like and what it held for us and we’ve all been told some kind of interesting thing about ourselves that has nothing to do with the art or our talent or our work or what we’ve given to our audition or whatever. That has nothing to do with anything.” Grande recently announced that she will be releasing the documentary “The Eternal Sunshine Diaries: The Making of the Tour, premiering on December 11, followed by the concert film “The Eternal Sunshine Tour” on December 12, exclusively on Peacock. She is currently on a press run in the lead-up to the release of “Focker-in-Law,” in theaters today. title: David Fincher Explains AI Use in ‘Cliff Booth’ and How AI Can Be Used on Film Sets to Reduce The Amount of Takes but Still Have ‘Real Human Beings’
full_text: × Nov 25, 2026 10:55am PT David Fincher Explains AI Use in ‘Cliff Booth’ and How AI Can Be Used on Film Sets to Reduce The Amount of Takes but Still Have ‘Real Human Beings’ By Corbin Bolies Plus Icon Corbin Bolies Latest Jensen Huang Reinstated as Nvidia CEO After Series of Affairs 2 days ago CAA’s Bryan Lourd Urges Congress to Pass NO FAKES Act to Combat AI Deepfakes: ‘Every One of Us Should Have the Right to Say No’ 4 days ago Late Comedian Sam Kinison — With His AI Avatar — Gears Up for Second Act with Buchwald (EXCLUSIVE) 5 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Getty Images David Fincher admitted in an interview published Wednesday that some AI was used in the post-production of “ The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth ,” but that it was all done to enhance the work of “real human beings.” Fincher appeared on The Ringer’s “Big Picture” podcast, where he told host Sean Fennessey that AI helped sync the best take of a line reading with the best performance take when they didn’t align on camera. Related Stories 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Extended Cut Sets December Release Date in Theaters 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Spins Up Massive Numbers for Sony's Quarterly Earnings “I feel like with the tools we now have,” Fincher said, before adding that the film only spent between four or five days of actors re-recording their dialogue above scenes. Only 5% of the film used “automated dialogue replacement, he said, while the rest was “all AI.” “We could use AI to re-lip that thing,” he added. “So it was freeing, it was the freeing up of…think of this entirely plastically. We’re not chiseling this out of marble. We’re working with plasticine. You know what I mean? Just giving ourselves that freedom to go, ‘what is the best thing on the eye, and then what is the best thing on the ear’ and fucking do not worry about how we’re going to get there, because we will figure out a way. And we did, in most cases. I think there’s a couple of shots [that] didn’t quite work, but they’re getting there. By the time it’s on service.” Fennessey premised his interview on the podcast by noting it took place before allegations regarding the use of generative AI on the film emerged, so he didn’t ask Fincher about other potential instances of AI in the film. Still, Fincher said he viewed AI as a tool that could help creatives focus on the work the technology can’t assist with, such as “sculpting, painting, aging, blowing fake spiders’ webs into the corner, smoking up a volume, putting a shaft of light in it” or “putting [a] crazy f—king wig on somebody.” “I can imagine a world where, and I don’t think we’re far away, you hire all the same people,” Fincher said. “You walk into a set that’s beautifully handcrafted and you hire all those people, and you shoot the master. You shoot the master 20, 25 times till you get worked out exactly.” Doing so, he said, can lower the intense amount of takes he’s known for, “because I won’t miss focus in AI. I will land a stick that all they shot in AI. And I will be able to make sure that hair doesn’t cross right in front of your cornea in AI.” “It’ll still be based on real human beings,” Fincher added. “It’ll still be based on real human, the way humans move and how they traverse a set and how they, how they pull up their trousers before they sit down or take their coat off. All that stuff will be there, people will only have to do it 15 times.” “Does working that way appeal to you?” Fennessey asked. “Totally,” Fincher replied. The comments came days after those who attended early screenings of the Netflix film, out in Imax theaters Wednesday, cited instances where generative AI appeared to have been used, including during a flashback scene where a horse carriage appeared to have two wagons. “What could have been a really great sequel is overshadowed by some of the most blatant and egregious AI use I’ve ever seen in a studio film,” Fincher and Netflix have not commented on those instances, though he told the Los Angeles Times in an interview published last week that he didn’t fear the emergence of AI as a filmmaking tool. “It exists. Should we not use it?” he said. “Is everyone satisfied that we have figured this art form out enough that what we really need to do is go back to celluloid?” Fincher added. “How long have people painted? 40,000 years? We’re talking about a thing that’s a hundred years old and everyone’s going, ‘Stop. Pencils down. No more iterating. It’s not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person’s eyes.’” Netflix has also been a proponent of AI in filmmaking, purchasing Ben Affleck’s AI tool startup InterPositive for $587 million in March and revealing in August that more than 300 programs in its catalog have used some level of generative AI this year. title: Bowen Yang, Mark Ruffalo and the Rise of Antisemitism in Hollywood
full_text: × Skip to main content By James Kirchick Plus Icon James Kirchick View All November 25, 2026 10:34am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Bowen Yang and Mark Ruffalo John Nacion/Variety/Getty Images; Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images Bowen Yang insists that he didn’t know “Zio” was an antisemitic slur . In a resurfaced clip from his Las Culturistas podcast, the comedian muttered the term under his breath at the mention of Regina Spektor , the Jewish American singer-songwriter. Yang was responding to a guest, another alleged wit named Edy Modica, who said that Spektor was “a little Israel, hard-core.” Spektor, who was born in the Soviet Union and immigrated to the United States as a child refugee, has been outspoken in her defense of the Jewish state since the Hamas massacre of Oct. 7, 2023, and given her personal history, is well attuned to left-wing antisemitism . When protestors interrupted one of her concerts last year screaming “Free Palestine ,” a visibly frustrated Spektor announced to the crowd, “The only reason I even speak English is because I came here to escape this shit.” Related Stories Movies Takashi Miike's 'Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo' From Neon Gets Early 2027 Release Lifestyle Veruschka, Mesmerizing Supermodel of the 1960s and '70s, Dies at 87 “Zio,” short for “Zionist,” was popularized by former KKK Grand Wizard David Duke when he was going through a respectability phase and needed a way to attack Jews without actually naming them as such. In his apology, Yang seemed sincerely shocked to hear this. “I want to genuinely apologize for using a word on the podcast without knowing its antisemitic history,” he wrote on Instagram. “Particularly upsetting to realize that I adopted language popularized by far-right movements whose rhetoric we should be wary of and act against.” We should take Yang at his word that he didn’t know the antisemitic etymology of “Zio.” Why would he? So profoundly antisemitic are the progressive cultural spaces Yang inhabits that people toss around racial slurs propagated by men in white hoods without a second thought. Does anyone really believe that Bowen Yang knows the first thing about the Israeli-Palestinian conflict? Like everyone in his social set, one that dominates large swaths of the entertainment world, he acquires his progressive worldview — to which vicious hatred of Israel is central — by osmosis. If there’s one issue that unites the far left and the far right in this country, it’s the Jewish Question. Yang seemed more distraught about the far-right origins of “Zio” than he did about the community the word intends to harm: Zionists, i.e. anyone who believes in the right of Israel to exist, i.e. the vast majority of the world’s Jews. In the minds of Yang and others of his ilk, progressives cannot be antisemitic, just as they cannot be anti-black, anti-woman, anti-gay, or anti-anybody. Bigotry, to them, is exclusively a right-wing phenomenon. Yang isn’t an antisemite, you see, he’s just an “anti-Zionist.” We know this because he ended his apology with the requisite “Free Palestine,” no expression of contrition over Jewish pain complete today without a nod to the movement that wants to eliminate the world’s only Jewish state. Sadly, Yang wasn’t the only celebrity to make an antisemitic outburst last week. Like Yang, who owes his career to a Jew (Lorne Michaels), Mark Ruffalo has become a very rich man playing a comic book character created by one (Stan Lee). That didn’t stop him from impugning the loyalty of the country’s highest ranking Jewish public official. “Israel is just one issue in a whole host of reasons Van Hollen is the right leader for our times,” Ruffalo tweeted in a post explaining his support for Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen becoming Senate Majority Leader over Chuck Schumer. “We need justice, we need leadership that follows the will of the people not entrenched religious beliefs and loyalties.” Schumer, in other words, cannot be trusted in a position of political leadership because he’s a Jew who cares about Israel, a class of Americans whose “loyalties” are suspect. Ruffalo subjects no other ethnic group to this scrutiny, just Jews. According to him, Schumer is less American that the guy with a “Van” in his surname. Again, this is the sort of stuff Gregory Peck’s character might have encountered in Gentlemen’s Agreement coming out of the mouth of a leading Hollywood liberal in the year 2026. At least David Duke has the courage to be forthright in his antisemitism. William Goldman’s famous maxim about Hollywood — “nobody knows anything” — applies just as much, if not more, to its denizens’ understanding of politics. It is amazing to me, after the popularity of Team America: World Police , Ricky Gervais’ numerous award show appearances and the Kamala Harris presidential campaign, that celebrities still have the nerve to opine about anything other than filmmaking and whatever gambling platform they’re being paid to promote. Does nepo baby Hannah Einbinder realize how ridiculous she sounds, ranting “never again for anyone” at a gay rights event in support of an Islamist political movement that murders homosexuals and uses rape as a weapon of war? Just as we don’t ask plumbers to clean our teeth, we shouldn’t rely on people who pretend for a living to inform our political views. That antisemitism is so rife in certain sectors of Hollywood — that stars can so casually invoke hoary old prejudices against Jews and not have to worry for their careers in the way they certainly would were they to slander any other minority — says two things about the entertainment industry. One: that while Hollywood was largely built by Jews (something the Academy Museum needed to be prodded into acknowledging ), it is certainly not controlled by them. And two: that in its understanding of prejudice, antisemitism is taken less seriously than other forms of bigotry. A tale of two Academy Awards ceremonies illustrates how far Hollywood has fallen in this regard. In 1978, the actress Vanessa Redgrave won an Oscar for her role in Julia , based on a book by the Stalinist writer Lillian Hellman. Standing outside the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion were members of the extremist Jewish Defense League protesting Redgrave over her advocacy for the Palestinian cause. Accepting her prize, Redgrave condemned the “Zionist hoodlums” outside, “whose behavior is an insult to the stature of Jews all over the world and to their great and heroic record of struggle against fascism and oppression.” The Good Jews, according to Redgrave, are those who fight her political battles. Bad ones support Israel. Redgrave was appropriately booed. But the real rebuke arrived when the director and screenwriter Paddy Chayefsky later took the stage to present an award. An actual veteran of the war against fascism and a vocal opponent of the Hollywood blacklist, Chayefsky had the bona fides to censure Redgrave for attempting to hijack the evening. “I’m sick and tired of people exploiting the occasion of the Academy Awards for the propagation of their own political propaganda,” he said, a line that could be uttered at every Oscar ceremony. “I would like to suggest to Miss Redgrave that her winning an Academy Award is not a pivotal moment in history, does not require a proclamation and a simple thank you would have sufficed.” Fast forward to 2024, when the director Jonathan Glazer accepted the Oscar for best international film , The Zone of Interest . After thanking the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum, Glazer, his two fellow Jewish co-producers behind him, declared, “Right now, we stand here as men who refute their Jewishness and the Holocaust being hijacked by an occupation which has led to conflict for so many innocent people.” Those grubby Jews, exploiting the Holocaust to perpetrate their own genocide. This time, however, Glazer was applauded for his appalling remarks. And when Steven Spielberg — director of Schindler’s List , founder of the Shoah Foundation, and one of the most powerful men in Hollywood — took the stage later in the evening, he said nothing. There are many ways to measure Hollywood’s decline. The lackluster quality of the films. The fall in theatrical attendance. The rise in algorithmic-inspired content. Here’s another: the deprecation and marginalization of the people whose creativity helped make it the envy of the world. James Kirchick is the author of Secret City: The Hidden History of Gay Washington. THR

title: Veruschka, Supermodel Who Appeared in ‘Blow-Up,’ ‘Casino Royale,’ Dies at 87
full_text: × Nov 25, 2026 10:28am PT Veruschka, Supermodel Who Appeared in ‘Blow-Up,’ ‘Casino Royale,’ Dies at 87 By Pat Saperstein Plus Icon Pat Saperstein Deputy Editor @Variety_PatS Latest Veruschka, Supermodel Who Appeared in ‘Blow-Up,’ ‘Casino Royale,’ Dies at 87 36 minutes ago Philip Rosenberg, Oscar-Winning Production Designer for ‘All That Jazz,’ Dies at 91 18 hours ago Why New Wave Music Won’t Go Away: New Documentary Explores How Synthesizers, MTV and Androgyny Built the Enduring Genre 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Conde Nast via Getty Images Veruschka, the striking 1960s and ’70s supermodel who inspired some of Richard Avedon ‘s most iconic images and appeared in films including Michelangelo Antonioni’s “Blow-Up,” has died. She was 87. Her death was confirmed by Germany’s Bild newspaper . Standing over six feet tall, “Veruschka, with her high forehead, sculptural cheekbones, and elongated limbs, was one of the decade’s most arresting presences, whatever aesthetic she took on,” wrote Vogue in its obituary. She appeared on 13 American Vogue covers. Related Stories Golden Globes: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Goes Comedy, ‘Dune 3’ Skips Box Office Achievement Category and More (EXCLUSIVE) 'Cliff Booth' First Reactions: Brad Pitt's Sequel Is an ‘Absolute Triumph’ and a ‘Wildly Entertaining’ ‘Love Letter’ to Hollywood Born Vera Gottliebe Anna Gräfin von Lehndorff-Steinort in East Prussia, she came from a family of aristocrats. Her father joined the German resistance and was executed when she was 5 years old for being involved in the plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler. She was discovered in Italy when she was an art student and became a model, and after meeting Eileen Ford in Paris, she moved to New York. In addition to her brief appearance as herself in the iconic 1966 film “Blow-Up,” she appeared in several other films including the 2006 version of “Casino Royale,” in Franc Roddam’s 1985 “The Bride” and in the 1970 “Salome.” In “Casino Royale,” Veruschka appears as one of only two female poker players at a table with Daniel Craig’s James Bond, Le Chiffre and Felix Leiter. She worked with top photographers including David Bailey, Irving Penn, Steven Meisel, Francesco Scavullo and Peter Beard, and worked for fashion houses including YSL, Helmut Lang and Paco Rabanne. Italian photographer Franco Rubartelli, who created many of the most arresting images of her, was her romantic partner for nine years. She returned to modeling several times in more recent years, including for Acne Studios in 2018. full_text: Skip to main content By Rick Porter Plus Icon Rick Porter Television Business Editor rickporter Follow Sign Up View All November 25, 2026 10:26am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Morfydd Clark (right) in 'The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power' season three. Ben Rothstein/Prime Logo text Two streaming shows starting new seasons after long breaks saw their U.S. viewing numbers fall off some compared to their most recent outings. The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power and Black Doves were two of the top three original series for the week of Jan. 9-15, but both drew smaller viewing time totals than their previous premiere weeks, both of which came in 2024. The Rings of Power had 866 million minutes of viewing for the the week on Prime Video, with 70 percent of that (about 606 million) devoted to the four episodes of season three that premiered Nov. 11. The 866 million minutes was off by 15 percent from 1.02 billion minutes for season two’s first week in August 2024. Related Stories TV TV Ratings: NBA Logs Winning Streak in First Month of the Season TV 'The Rings of Power' Officially Renewed for Season 4 With Showrunners Returning Black Doves , meanwhile, scored 580 million viewing minutes with its season two premiere on Netflix, down 35 percent from its series debut (899 million) in December 2024. Internal viewing data reported by the two streamers also show declines for the two series: In renewing The Rings of Power for a fourth season, Prime Video said 33 million viewers worldwide had watched some of the new season over its first 12 days, compared to 40 million over 11 days for season two. Netflix reported 6.6 million global views for season two of Black Doves for the week; season one had 10.8 million for its first week. The No. 2 original series for the week was Marvel’s VisionQuest , which hit a high of 696 million viewing minutes on Disney+ for the week of its finale. Three shows made their chart debuts: Netflix’s The Body (498 million minutes), Hulu’s The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives: Orange County (461 million) and Peacock’s The Good Daughter (398 million). From continued its hot streak, leading the overall rankings for a fourth consecutive week with 1.55 billion minutes of watch time. The MGM+ series has now racked up 6.92 billion minutes of viewing since its first three seasons were added to Netflix in October. Tyler Perry’s The Gospel of Christmas led the movie top 10 with 372 million minutes of watch time for Netflix. Avengers: Endgame (315 million on Disney+) reappeared on the charts as the run-up to Avengers: Doomsday kicked into a higher gear. Nielsen’s streaming ratings cover viewing on TV sets only and don’t include minutes watched on computers or mobile devices. The ratings only measure U.S. audiences. title: BlackStar’s Luminary Gala Returns For Fourth Edition; Mahershala Ali & Mara Brock Akil Among Honorary Award Winners
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News 'Avengers: Doomsday' Tracking For All-Time Best $270M+ Opening Next Month; 'Dune 3' Eyes $75M+ Debut Read the full story By Zac Ntim Zac Ntim International Reporter @ZacharyNtim More Stories By Zac Jimmy Jenkins’s ‘God With Us,’ Starring Rotimi & Lil Rel Howery, Lands PVOD Release Allison Janae Hamilton Launches Production Outfit Swampwife Pictures & Sets ‘Holler’ Starring Edwina Findley & Valerie June As First Project Samantha Morton To Receive BFI Fellowship View All November 25, 2026 10:18am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Mahershala Ali BlackStar Projects. Mahershala Ali and Mara Brock Akil were among the honorary award winners at the BlackStar Projects’ Luminary Gala, which returned for its fourth edition on November 20 at The Bellevue Hotel in Philadelphia. Cinematographer John Simmons and Stanley Nelson and Marcia Smith’s Firelight Media were also among those honored with career awards on the evening. BlackStar Projects, the parent organization of the BlackStar Film Festival , hosts the gala, which also serves as a fundraiser for the film festival. The BlackStar Film Festival celebrated its 15th anniversary in August. Previous honorees include Mira Nair, Menelik Shabazz, Ava DuVernay, Julie Dash, Autumn Durald Arkapaw, and Wu-Tang’s RZA. Related Stories News Caron Creighton On Capturing The Fight To Save Northern California's Largest Homeless Encampment With Her Debut Feature 'Wood Street' News Haile Gerima Dissects His 10 Hour Documentary Feature 'Black Lions - Roman Wolves' & Teases His Next Project On America's Black Maroons “It’s really incredible to be here with you at our fourth annual Luminary Gala and in the BlackStar Film Festival’s 15th year,” Maori Karmael Holmes, founder, chief executive, and artistic officer of BlackStar Projects, said as she opened the evening’s festivities. Watch on Deadline “Back in 2012, we were all volunteers trying to put together a one-time event to celebrate the best of Black cinema from around the world. I couldn’t have imagined being here in 2026, in front of such illustrious guests, with BlackStar producing not only the festival, but also our print journal, an annual seminar at Stanford, and dozens of year-round screenings—all led by a truly brilliant staff.” Ali, who arrived at the gala fresh off the global rollout of his latest feature, Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother, also reminisced on the early iterations of the BlackStar Film Festival as he took the stage to receive his honorary award. Ali was introduced by André Holland. “I’m moved to tears. BlackStar, Maori Holmes—thank you for having me. It’s an honor to be here,” Ali began. “I got to visit years ago, in 2014, and witness the festival in its early years. It was amazing then, so I can’t imagine what it’s like now.” Ali continued, telling the audience that he arrived at the gala asking himself, “How did I get to a place where someone would feel I was worthy of this kind of love and honor?” “I kept going back to my own luminaries, and one in particular: my grandmother. She’s 92, and she’s the light in my eyes. She’s like my best friend,” Ali said, before emotionally recalling how his grandmother helped instill confidence in him as a young kid growing up in Hayward, California. Mahershala Ali on stage at the BlackStar Luminary Gala. Credit: BlackStar Projects. “She’d have me repeat after her: I’m handsome. I’m intelligent. I can do anything I put my mind to. I can be anything I want to be,” Ali recalled. Ali said his grandmother was also one of the first supporters of his decision to pursue acting. “This was 30 years ago, almost to the day. I was working at a record industry magazine for minimum wage, which was about $4.50 an hour at the time. I was trying to figure out what I was doing with my life,” Ali said. “After spending the summer at the California Shakespeare Festival, I knew passionately that I wanted a shot at acting. I was auditioning for NYU, and I’d told my grandparents many times that they only accept about 18 kids from around the country, so pray for me.” Some months before his NYU audition, Ali said, his grandmother returned from the grocery store with bundles of sweats and jumpers. “I said, What are those for? She said, You’re going to need these when you move to New York,’ Ali recalled. “She has been my light. I’m so grateful to my mother, of course, but my grandmother—what she’s done for me over my 50-some-odd years on this earth is guide me to have real belief in myself and my God-given talents,” he said. “She taught me to try to be of service to others and to something larger than myself, to try to be a generous actor every day, and to want for others what I want for myself. I try to embody those things. They all come from the best grandmother in the world, Mamie Gilmore.” Fireflight CEO Loira Limbal and Rafiah Vitalis, the company’s Senior Director of Finance and Operations, accepted the honorary award on stage for Nelson and Smith, who were also in attendance. Loira Limbal and Rafiah Vitalis with Stanley Nelson and Marcia Smith. Credit: BlackStar Projects. The company is a nonprofit organization that supports, resources, and advocates on behalf of documentary filmmakers of color. Fireflight is best known for its Documentary Lab . Accepting the honorary award, Limbal and Vitalis paid tribute to Nelson and Smith. “26 years ago, our co-founders sat down with the simple, stubborn idea that the stories of our communities deserve to be told by filmmakers from those communities and those filmmakers deserve support, mentorship, and a place to build,” Vitalis said. “Everything we are is thanks to you two.” Limbal and Vitalis said Fireflight was born out of a long tradition of socially conscious Black and Indigenous non-fiction filmmaking. “Our work is to carry that tradition forward, not as a tribute or memory, but as a continuation,” Vitalis said, adding, in union with Limbal: “To every filmmaker in this room, keep holding the camera, keep framing the questions, keep the archive.” Next up on the BlackStar calendar is the Greaves Seminar, a symposium for Black, Brown, and Indigenous film artists at Stanford. The seventh edition of the seminar takes place from March 5-7, 2027. Check out images from last week’s Luminary Gala below. Mara Brock Akil with Maori Karmael Holmes. Credit: BlackStar Projects. John Simmons with cinematographer Shawn Peters. Credit: BlackStar Projects. Mahershala Ali with André Holland and Maori Karmael Holmes. The sequel Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo stars Lily James and Godzilla vs. Kong ’s Shun Oguri in a new take on the seedy and corrupt detective who first appeared in Abel Ferrara’s 1992 original neo-noir crime drama with Harvey Keitel as the Lieutenant. That was followed by Werner Herzog ’s 2009 film Bad Lieutenant: Port of Call New Orleans , starring Nicolas Cage and Eva Mendes. Neon acquired the U.S. rights to Miike’s third franchise outing that centers on a Tokyo cop (Oguri) steeped in gambling debt and a drug addiction and paired with an FBI agent, played by James, to search for a missing politician’s daughter (Liv Morgan) in Tokyo’s Yakuza criminal underworld. Japanese maestro Miike is best known for movies like Audition , the Yakuza trilogy Dead Or Alive and thriller Ichi The Killer , along with Sukiyaki Western Django, Visitor Q, 13 Assassins and his 100th film, Blade of the Immortal. Miike also has an upcoming slasher-horror film starring Charli xcx, Milly Alcock, Norman Reedus, Kiko Mizuhara and Show Kasamatsu. Bad Lieutenant: Tokyo had a world premiere at the Toronto Film Festival and will hit theaters on the same weekend as Pixar’s Gatto and Michael Jordan’s new take on The Thomas Crown Affair. title: As ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Opens on Just 200 Imax Screens, Netflix’s Movie Theater Push Is Still Failing Moviegoers
full_text: × Nov 25, 2026 10:15am PT As ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Opens on Just 200 Imax Screens, Netflix’s Movie Theater Push Is Still Failing Moviegoers By Owen Gleiberman Plus Icon Owen Gleiberman Chief Film Critic @OwenGleiberman Latest ‘Hershey’ Review: In a Sugary Sweet Biopic, Finn Wittrock Plays the Candy Man Who Turned Chocolate Into an American Empire 13 hours ago ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Review: Brad Pitt Hits the Aura Jackpot in a Very Fun Tarantino Hangout Movie That Feels Like QT TV 6 days ago ‘Madden’ Review: Nicolas Cage Plays John Madden as the Disheveled Buddha of Football in David O. Russell’s Eccentric Stunt of a Sports Biopic 1 week ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Courtesy of Netflix © 2026 If you’re a fan of Quentin Tarantino and David Fincher and Brad Pitt , and you loved “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” and have your heart set on seeing that film’s sequel, the highly entertaining (and appropriately well-reviewed) “ The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth ,” over Thanksgiving weekend, I have a scientific phrase to describe your predicament: You’re shit out of luck. But let me qualify that. If you’re lucky enough to live near one of the 200 Imax screens on which “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” will be playing, you can see the movie this weekend. Everyone else will have to wait until Dec. 23, when the film drops on Netflix. Sound familiar? It’s the old Netflix theater-and-streaming bait-and-switch, with the eagerly awaited movie in question being “released in theaters”…but also held back. (The film will play in theaters for just two weeks.) We’re getting the slightly better version of the formula this time. For years, the Netflix game plan was to open a movie for an awards-qualifying run on an astoundingly small number of screens, the majority of them in New York and Los Angeles. The media tended to treat each of these “releases” as bigger than it was, for the funny reason that most entertainment reporters live in New York or L.A., which leads them to think, “Hey, it’s playing at a theater near me!” In the case of “The Further Mis-Adventures,” perception may trump reality, as an Imax release has the aura of being something special. In this case, the Imax release doesn’t hinge on the movie possessing some outsize visual magic. If anything, “The Further Mis-Adventures” represents the moment when the Tarantino aesthetic got fused with the karma of television . No, the Imax release is all about a deal that was cut months ago, after Netflix decided to bump the release of Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” from Thanksgiving weekend to Feb. 12, 2027. “Narnia” was originally set to occupy those 200 Imax screens (and only those screens), but Gerwig, using her post–”Barbie” clout, insisted on a larger-scale release. Ted Sarandos, the co-CEO of Netflix, caved on that one (Gerwig kind of had him over a barrel), and decided to placate the exhibitors by agreeing to swap “The Further Mis-Adventures” into the Thanksgiving/Imax slot. In his mind, that would make everyone happy. “The Further Mis-Adventures” is being positioned as an Imax “event” — though here’s how Netflix, once again, has missed the forest for the trees. The company has been through a dicey year, with Sarandos foiled in his attempt to acquire Warner Bros. — a rare humiliating public defeat for him. And the fact that so many members of the entertainment industry questioned Sarandos’s commitment to theatrical was arguably why that deal didn’t feel right. There was a fear in Hollywood that a Netflix/Warner Bros. merger could kill the business of theatrical moviegoing as we know it. (Whatever misgivings one might have about Skydance or its leader, David Ellison, for some they represented the healthier alternative — or maybe just the lesser of two evils.) In the wake of that defeat, Sarandos declared that Netflix, going forward, would be pivoting more toward theatrical, on a case-by-case basis. What that would actually mean remained to be seen. But the release of “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” stands as a powerful indicator, since the desire to see this movie is so strong. In July of 2019, “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” enjoyed an opening weekend of $41 million. A highly anticipated sequel will tend to outperform the original film. That means that “The Further Mis-Adventures,” had it opened on 3,500 screens (matching the screen count of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood”), could likely have netted at least $50 million, in the U.S. alone, over the five-day weekend. This raises the inevitable question: Why isn’t “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” opening on 3,500 screens? Imax is fine, but what about eyeballs? The answer, in a way, is simple: That kind of release still isn’t part of the Netflix DNA. Yet just stand back for a moment and consider, on basic populist moviegoing terms, the slightly absurd aspect of this situation, the way that it is simply not serving moviegoers . “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” is an unusual Tarantino film, in that he wrote it and didn’t direct it, but it’s still every inch a QT joint. Fincher, who did direct it, has a powerful following of his own. (Their collaboration represents a rock-star mash-up.) And what of Brad Pitt, in the best role he has had in a decade — the one role that’s ever won him an acting Oscar? Pitt is still a dazzling old-school movie star, and if you’re wondering if his highly publicized offscreen travails have hurt him at the box office, check out the grosses for his latest movie, “Heart of the Beast.” It’s just a man-and-his-dog wilderness adventure film, and it’s coming up on a take of $70 million. Based on that, I’d say “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” would have killed. The movie has a budget of $120 million, which raises the age-old question: Why is Ted Sarandos so willing to leave money on the table? But there’s now an age-old answer: That’s the way Sarandos preserves his business model. Let’s imagine an alternate universe in which Netflix released “The Further Mis-Adventures” on 3,500 screens, and by the time its run was over it had grossed $140 million (matching the domestic tally of “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood”). If that had happened, prestige directors signing up with Netflix would be upping the pressure for full-scale theatrical releases. The whole era is now exerting that pressure, with sleeper smashes like “You Can See Everything,” “Obsession,” and “Backrooms” acting as a nearly mythological advertisement for the comeback of theatrical. The fact that Fincher himself, after years of working closely with Netflix (on “The Killer” and “Mank,” and on the celebrated series “Mindhunter”), announced in September that he won’t be renewing his exclusive overall deal with the company is a move that feels hugely symbolic. We’ll see what the further mis-adventures of Netflix bring. When it comes to theatrical, can Netflix truly change its spots? Much will be riding on Peter Rice, the company’s new chief content officer. With his golden track record from the Fox Searchlight days, he has long been bullish on theatrical. If he hires Mike DeLuca and Pam Abdy, those high-powered refugees of Skydance, or even if Rice just oversees the film side himself (as he has suggested he might), it could mark a new era for Netflix. But based on the strangely limited release of “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” a movie that audiences are hungry for but in most cases wlll not be able to see in theaters, I won’t be holding my breath, even as the constricted Netflix theatrical model now looks like it’s swimming perilously upstream. title: Jane Fonda, Robert De Niro & Other Figures Sign Letter Backing Chris Van Hollen For Majority Leader — Amid A Chuck Schumer Aide’s Prank
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News 'Avengers: Doomsday' Tracking For All-Time Best $270M+ Opening Next Month; 'Dune 3' Eyes $75M+ Debut Read the full story By Ted Johnson Ted Johnson Political Editor @tedstew More Stories By Ted Al Gore To Purchase Hometown Paper Carthage Courier MS NOW Hosts Sign On To Letter Urging Adoption Of “Fair” WGAE Contract; Network Says Talks Are Ongoing And “Constructive” Skydance Buyouts Impact CBS Stations; Local Chicago Anchor Among Those Departing View All November 25, 2026 10:03am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Senators Chris Van Hollen and Chuck Schumer Jemal Countess/Getty Images for MoveOn Civic Action; Tom Brenner for The Washington Post/Pool Jane Fonda , Robert De Niro and Chelsea Handler are among the entertainment figures who have signed on to a letter backing Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-MD) in his bid to become Senate majority leader over Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-NY). The letter, signed by about three dozen figures describing themselves as donors, fundraisers and artists, stated that in this year’s midterms, “voters delivered not on ly a mandate but an opportunity for change: a government that delivers real value in the daily lives of working families.” “That change will only come from renewed leadership with a vision for the future,” the letter stated. “The Democratic Party has a trust and credibility problem, and fixing it requires Senate leaders willing to challenge the entrenched interests and power structures that protect those in power, in both parties.” The letter also called on senators to support candidates “who are dedicated to accountability, transparency and the bold agenda voters demanded.” Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Al Gore To Purchase Hometown Paper Carthage Courier News MS NOW Hosts Sign On To Letter Urging Adoption Of "Fair" WGAE Contract; Network Says Talks Are Ongoing And "Constructive" The election for majority leader, to be held early next month, has highlighted party divisions, including among donors and in the entertainment industry, and even after the whopping victories of Democrats across the country in the midterms. Noting that the upcoming vote on a Senate leader will be chosen by secret ballot, the letter called on the caucus to support Van Hollen, who is challenging Schumer, the current minority leader who had been the presumptive favorite to win following Democrats huge gains in which they flipped control of the chamber. Others who signed on to the letter include Bruce Cohen, Padma Lakshmi, Laurie David, David Mandel, Fisher Stevens, Marisa Tomei, Amy Ziering and Morgan Spector. In a statement. De Niro said, “Americans voted for the change necessary to fight the corruption, cruelty, and policies of Trump and his Epstein class cronies. That’s why I’m supporting change in Senate leadership. Chris Van Hollen is a progressive leader and a fierce fighter. He’s the right person to lead the Senate majority.” Van Hollen has pitched his candidacy as a necessary response to the midterm results and that Democrats’ unexpected gains were also calls for change, coming from the left and the middle of the party. “The voters responsible for the Blue Tsunami want fundamental change and bold, new ideas. Simply put, Chuck Schumer is the past and Chris Van Hollen is the present and the future,” Cohen said. Schumer has insisted that he will emerge victorious, and even some entertainment industry observers believe that he will return to the post. Mathew Littman, who leads The Working Group, which organizes Hollywood creatives, said via email, “Senator Schumer just led one of the great political wins of all time. He earned two years to lead his fellow Senate Democrats.” A Times analysis last week showed that Schumer had the public support of 16 senators and Van Hollen had the backing of 6, with 4 more calling for change. But more than two dozen senators’ backing is unknown. Spokespersons for Schumer and Van Hollen did not return requests for comment. But a campaign aide to Schumer, Angelo Roefaro, told Politico that he was behind a bit of pranks-manship in advance of the release of the letter. He gained access to the Google doc draft of the letter and added Frank Sinatra’s name to the list of signatories, and subbed in Schumer’s name for Van Hollen. A Times reporter initially posted a copy of the letter endorsing Van Hollen, but with Sinatra’s name still included, before replacing it with an image of the corrected letter, per Politico. title: Veruschka, Mesmerizing Supermodel of the 1960s and ’70s, Dies at 87
full_text: Skip to main content By Mike Barnes Plus Icon Mike Barnes Senior Editor mikebarnes4 Follow Sign Up View All November 25, 2026 9:58am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Veruschka Franco Rubartelli/Condé Nast/Getty Images Veruschka, the chameleonic, long-limbed supermodel and performance artist who photographer Richard Avedon once pronounced “the most beautiful woman in the world,” has died. She was 87. Veruschka died in her home in Berlin, the German newspaper Bild reported. On Instagram, her former partner and photographer Franco Rubartelli acknowledged her death and noted “she wasn’t just a great model. She was an elegant woman, sensitive, brave, with a beauty that did not stay in the camera, it would get into the soul of whoever watched her. Related Stories Lifestyle "Sometimes You Just Have to Think: 'What Will Make People Laugh?'": Lolly Adefope on Gags, 'Ghosts' and Her West End Debut Movies Ava DuVernay to Receive London Critics' Circle Inaugural Laura Mulvey Female Trailblazer Award “She had a way of being in the world that you don’t learn; you take in. People like Veruschka don’t go away at all. They stay in a picture, in a perfume, in a song, in a way of smiling.” One of the first supermodels, Veruschka in the 1960s and ‘70s appeared often on covers of Vogue and other magazines around the globe. With a high forehead, blue-eyed gaze and sculptured, distinctive cheekbones, she stood more than six feet tall and was a muse for designers including Karl Lagerfeld , Yves Saint Laurent and Valentino . “What made the German model so mesmerizing was her seeming disinterest in preserving any one iteration of that beauty,” Anna Cafolla wrote in Vogue . “She could be imperious or impish, feral or feline, androgynous or opulently feminine. She could contort her impossibly long limbs into unreal configurations, traversing fashion magazines and the wider public’s consciousness with ease in a way that had never been done before.” Vogue offers a look at her “most striking beauty looks of all time” here . Veruschka did her first shoot wearing nothing but body paint in 1966, and after she left modeling in 1975, she collaborated with German sculptor-painter Holger Trülzsch for a series of avant-garde self-portrait photographs in which her painted figure dissolved into forests or sides of buildings. On the big screen, she appeared as a version of herself in Michelangelo Antonioni’s Blow-Up (1966) when she’s photographed by David Hemmings’ character in London in the Swinging ’60s, and she had a brief turn as a high-stakes poker player in Casino Royale (2006). Veruschka was photographed by Franco Rubartelli for Vogue in 1968. Franco Rubartelli/Condé Nast/Getty Images Vera Gottliebe Anna Gräfin von Lehndorff-Steinort was born on May 14, 1939, in Königsberg, East Prussia (now Kaliningrad, Russia). She was 5 when her father, Count Heinrich von Lehndorff-Steinort, was executed in September 1944 for his involvement in a plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler two months earlier. Her mother, Gottliebe, was sent to a prison camp as she and her three sisters were forced to live in a Nazi children’s home. After moving from Hamburg, Germany, she was an art student in Florence when she was discovered in 1959 by photographer Ugo Mulas; before long, she was a full-time model, working in Paris, New York and Munich. She reinvented herself with a new name and returned to New York, where she found a champion in Diana Vreeland, then editor-in-chief of Vogue . “I dressed all in black,” she recalled, “and went to see all the top photographers, like Irving Penn, and said, ‘I am Veruschka who comes from the border between Russia, Germany and Poland. I’d like to see what you can do with my face.’” She appeared on 13 covers of Vogue ’s American edition and on the covers of its Italian, French and British editions as well. Along the way, she was photographed by the likes of Avedon, Penn, Rubartelli, Peter Beard, Francesco Scavullo, Horst P. Horst and David Bailey and became one of the highest-paid, most in-demand models of her generation. She graced the cover of Life magazine in 1967, and a year later, Rubartelli famously shot her in a lace-up safari jacket from Yves Saint Laurent for French Vogue . In 1971, she was the subject of the Rubartelli-directed fantasy film Veruschka — Poetry of a Woman and appeared in the West German magazine Stern with 27 other women under the cover line “Wir haben abgetrieben!” (“We’ve had abortions!”) to advocate for legal abortions. She returned to the runway for Chanel in 1994, for Giles Deacon’s spring show in London in 2011 and for an Acne Studios lookbook in 2017. Her autobiography, Veruschka — Mein Leben , was published in 2011. Her beauty, Avedon said, “demands something, and you must extend yourself to meet the challenge or know that a kind of splendor is lost to you forever.” View this post on Instagram THR

title: ‘Twilight’ Director ‘Almost Fell Out of Bed’ Over Robert Pattinson’s Bond Casting: ‘The Same Bed Where Rob and Kristen Stewart Auditioned Their Kiss’
full_text: × Nov 25, 2026 9:51am PT ‘Twilight’ Director ‘Almost Fell Out of Bed’ Over Robert Pattinson’s Bond Casting: ‘The Same Bed Where Rob and Kristen Stewart Auditioned Their Kiss’ By Zack Sharf Plus Icon Zack Sharf Digital News Director ZSharf Latest ‘Twilight’ Director ‘Almost Fell Out of Bed’ Over Robert Pattinson’s Bond Casting: ‘The Same Bed Where Rob and Kristen Stewart Auditioned Their Kiss’ 1 hour ago ‘To Me, My X-Men’: James Marsden Says It Was ‘Important’ for Cyclops to Be a Leader in ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ After Taking a ‘Back Seat to Wolverine’ 23 hours ago Adam Driver: ‘No One Was Paying Us’ to Develop ‘The Hunt for Ben Solo’ and ‘Star Wars’ Boss Said ‘We Have a 100% Approval’ to Make It, Then Disney Killed It 2 days ago See All Add us as a Google Preferred Source Bond: Amazon Studios / MGM; Twilight: Summit Entertainment/courtesy Everett Collection “ Twilight ” director Catherine Hardwicke appeared on “The Kyle Buchanan Show” and weighed in on Robert Pattinson ‘s buzzy casting as the new James Bond actor. Hardwicke is largely responsible for shooting Pattinson’s career into the stratosphere by casting him as the vampire Edward Cullen opposite Kristen Stewart as Bella Swan in 2008’s “Twilight.” Flash forward nearly 20 years and Pattinson is now set to become the movies’ most iconic secret agent. “I almost fell out of my bed,” Hardwicke said about the moment she found out about Pattinson’s Bond casting. “I just didn’t think they were going to choose him because of ‘The Batman’ and he’s so famous and they like to get the unknown [actor]. I did almost fall out of the bed, and that is the same bed that Rob and Kristen auditioned for the first time and did their kissing scene. It was kind of bizarre. He fell out of the bed when he did the audition and landed on the floor, so it was kind of cool.” Related Stories Jo Koy on ‘Blue in the Face,’ Steven Spielberg, Biggie’s Mom and Learning What His Name Really Means at Long John Silver’s 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Extended Cut Sets December Release Date in Theaters Hardwicke added, “He’s intense and interesting and has got a lot of stuff going on in there. He’s weird and he’s original. He does not fit the mold. He’s not afraid to say crazy shit, that’s what I love about it.” Pattinson and Stewart auditioned for “Twilight” together at Hardwicke’s home, where the director was interested to see whether or not the actors had the kind of instant chemistry that was required for Edward and Bella. “[Rob] walked in and he had his hair dyed black for some play, with these wacky bangs. He was a bit out of shape. His shirt was just all messy, and I’m like, ‘Oh, okay. Okay, let’s see how this goes,’” Hardwicke told “The Big Hit Show” podcast in 2022, noting that Pattinson got “so into” the kissing scene with Stewart that he “he fell off the bed.” “I’m like, ‘Dude, calm down.’ And I’m in there filming with my little video camera, whatever…In the end, Kristen was like, ‘It has to be Rob,’” the director added. “I could tell they had a lot of chemistry, and I’m like, ‘Oh my God.’ I thought, Kristen was 17. I don’t want to get in some illegal things. So I remember I told Rob, ‘By the way, Kristen is 17. In our country, it’s illegal to have a sexual…’ And he’s like, ‘Oh, okay, whatever.’” Stewart remembered the audition while speaking to The New Yorker in 2021, saying: ”[Pattinson had an] intellectual approach that was combined with ‘I don’t give a fuck about this, but I’m going to make this sing.’ And I was, like, ‘Ugh, same.’ And, whatever, we were young and stupid and, not to say that we made it so much better, but that’s what it needed, and that’s what anybody playing those parts needed to feel.” When Pattinson’s Bond casting was announced earlier this month, “Twilight” fans took to social media to note how the franchise predicted the news. In a scene from Hardwicke’s original movie, Justin Chon’s character, Eric Yorkie, passes out flyers to his fellow high schoolers and notes this year’s prome theme as he announces Forks High School’s prom theme is Monte Carlo, adding: “Gambling, tuxedos and Bond. James Bond.” The camera that cuts to Pattinson’s Edward Cullen. “You probably saw that scene online where we say, ‘Bond, James Bond,’ and then we cut to Rob. That’s the one scene where I was like, ‘Let’s put the sunglasses on,'” Hardwicke said in her latest interview. “He got out of the car and he looked so suave that he inspired the line, ‘Bond, James Bond.’ It was cool. We did think he looked like James Bond. I guess we were seeing the future.” Watch Hardwicke’s full appearance on “The Kyle Buchanan Show” in the video below. title: Watch Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Full In-Depth Breakdown of ‘You Can See Everything’
full_text: Skip to main content By David Canfield Plus Icon David Canfield Senior Entertainment Writer View All November 25, 2026 9:47am Add us as a Google Preferred Source From left: Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder speak with THR's David Canfield during a 'You Can See Everything' Q&A at the 2026 SCAD Savannah Film Festival in October. Jason Kempin/Getty Images for SCAD [This article contains spoilers for You Can See Everything ] When Lance Oppenheim first told his buddy Nathan Fielder that he heard about the potential to make a new documentary about Elizabeth Holmes’ last days before going to prison, Fielder wasn’t sure what tale there was left to tell. There were other docs, books and an Emmy-winning Hulu series out there about her. “I was interested in her, but I didn’t really think there was a story there to do, especially for a doc,” Fielder said last month from the SCAD Savannah Film Festival , where he and Oppenheim joined The Hollywood Reporter for a special post-screening live Q&A (watch it in full below). Related Stories Movies 'You Can See Everything' Now Streaming: Where to Watch Nathan Fielder's Elizabeth Holmes Doc Online SCAD Savannah Film Festival David Greaves Says 'Once Upon a Time in Harlem' Is "An Act of Resistance" Against Efforts to Erase Black History Oppenheim remembered Fielder asking, “Hasn’t there been a billion things made about this person already?” And he replied, “Yes — but maybe there’s something else.” To say that has proven true would be the understatement of this film season. Moving in with Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans , in her final weeks of freedom — then continuing to make their movie in increasingly daring and surprising directions — Oppenheim and Fielder teamed up for You Can See Everything , one of the most successful theatrical documentaries of all time and a bona fide cultural phenomenon. The movie offers compellingly slippery portraits of both Holmes and Evans, plays off Fielder’s noted screen persona to fascinating effect and features a plum secret role for Amanda Seyfried, who won awards for her portrayal of Holmes in The Dropout (and is now a wildcard Oscar contender). But perhaps most fundamentally, it’s a singular synthesis of what Fielder and Oppenheim have brought to their work over their last several years, toying with true-story formats in projects as diverse as Primetime and The Rehearsal . “I feel like the two of us are both interested in the challenges of capturing authentic life on camera,” Oppenheim said. “He’s coming at it from a different angle, and I’m coming at it from a different angle too.” Their SCAD Docs to Watch conversation finds the two directors going in-depth on their process from beginning to end on You Can See Everything — including the conversations that led to Seyfried’s participation and the biggest questions they’re still wrestling with, months after completing the movie. Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything . Courtesy of Everett Collection Indeed, the movie has left most every viewer with questions. This dynamic was what motivated Fielder and Oppenheim to make the movie in the first place — after only a bit of time spent with Holmes and Evans, it was clear the surreal nature of the arrangement was too rich to ignore. “There were these moments that would happen in the house that we would all witness with our eyes, but when we talked about it at the end of the day, Lance and I would have vastly different ideas of what was actually happening and what was going on — and then we talked to the rest of the crew and everyone had different ideas about that,” Fielder said. “It was then that we were like, ‘Wow, if we can’t all agree on this, maybe there’s something to this idea.’” Watch the full conversation above. You Can See Everything is in theaters and available for purchase on digital platforms. THR

title: ‘Top Gear’ Sets 2028 Return — With Gordon Ramsay as Host
full_text: Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All November 25, 2026 9:21am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Gordon Ramsay and The Stig for 'Top Gear.' Courtesy of BBC Studios Logo text If you can’t stand the heat … get behind the wheel? Top Gear is set to return to the BBC with entrepreneur, chef and self-proclaimed car fanatic Gordon Ramsay as its host. The U.K.’s beloved, long-running series has been off air since 2022 after co-host Andrew Flintoff was involved in an on-set car crash. He suffered serious facial and rib injuries when his open-top vehicle overturned on Top Gear ‘s test track. On Wednesday, the broadcaster confirmed that the world’s most celebrated motoring entertainment show (previously helmed by Jeremy Clarkson, James May and Richard Hammond) will be back on our screens in 2028. Related Stories Movies How 'The Other Bennet Sister' Defied the Odds as a Smash Hit Lifestyle "Sometimes You Just Have to Think: 'What Will Make People Laugh?'": Lolly Adefope on Gags, 'Ghosts' and Her West End Debut Produced by BBC Studios , the all-new series will see Ramsay take the steering wheel, “setting the agenda and leading an all-new lineup of co-presenters through epic adventures, daring tests and spectacular stunts in pursuit of the stories, machines and mayhem that generations of viewers have come to expect and love from the show.” Filming will take place across the U.K. and around the world in 2027, with the iconic Top Gear Test Track at Dunsfold Aerodrome in Surrey once again serving as the show’s home and base. Top Gear ’s tame racing driver, The Stig, will also be returning to support the new series in the usual understated way. Ramsay is no stranger to the show, having been a guest previously on three occasions: in the show’s first series in 2002, its eighth series in 2006 and its 23rd series in 2017. Each appearance saw him showcase his driving skills with a lap of the track — his fastest time clocking in at a blistering one minute and 46.3 seconds behind the wheel of a Chevrolet Lacetti — earning him 7th place on Top Gear’s ‘Star In A Reasonably Priced Car’ leaderboard. “My love affair with cars began as a child, growing up a field away from Silverstone, where I would climb over the fences and sneak in for a glimpse of the racing,” began Ramsay. “That early excitement sparked a lifelong passion for cars, motor sport, beautiful design and extraordinary engineering. At its very best Top Gear has always been about the unexpected — surprising, entertaining and just the right amount of chaos. That’s the spirit we want to build on, bringing a fresh energy and ambition to create something truly thrilling for a whole new generation of audiences. It’s an incredibly exciting opportunity, and I genuinely can’t wait to get started!” Top Gear is produced by BBC Studios Entertainment Productions for BBC One and BBC iPlayer and was commissioned by Ed Havard, director of entertainment and Michael Jochnowitz, head of constructed reality and studio entertainment. For BBC Studios, the creative director is Mel Balac, the showrunner is Rowland French, and the executive producer is Zac Assemakis. Suzy Lamb is managing director for BBC Studios Entertainment. THR

title: Gordon Ramsay To Host Revived ‘Top Gear’ For BBC
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News 'Avengers: Doomsday' Tracking For All-Time Best $270M+ Opening Next Month; 'Dune 3' Eyes $75M+ Debut Read the full story By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max Gordon Ramsay To Host Revived ‘Top Gear’ For BBC Netflix Only Big Player Not Funding UK’s Independent Bullying & Harassment Complaints Body UK Actors Union Equity To Kickstart Negotiations With Streamers Early Next Year View All November 25, 2026 9:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Top Gear' BBC Gordon Ramsay is shifting from the kitchen to the race track. The superstar chef has been unveiled as the next host of the BBC ’s Top Gear , coming four years after Andrew Flintoff ’s crash. Ramsay will lead the series and set the agenda alongside a soon-to-be-announced lineup of co-presenters and with iconic racing driver The Stig returning. Filming will take place across the UK and around the world in 2027, with the Top Gear test track at Dunsfold Aerodrome in Surrey once again serving as the show’s home and base. Related Stories News BBC Journalists Vote To Take Strike Action Over Job Cuts News The BBC's Latest Idea To Save £500M: Bring In Consultants Ramsay is no stranger to Top Gear , having been a guest previously on three occasions. Each appearance saw him showcase his driving skills, with one earning him seventh place on Top Gear’s ‘Star In A Reasonably Priced Car’ leaderboard. Watch on Deadline The modern iteration of Top Gear aired on the BBC for 20 years before Flintoff’s “life-altering” crash at the Dunsfold Aerodrome ground it to a halt. It was rested “for the foreseeable future” in late 2023 after Flintoff agreed a reported £9M ($11.8M) settlement with producer BBC Studios . In recent months, talk of a return had been rife and this was officially confirmed at the Edinburgh TV Festival by BBC entertainment chief Ed Havard. At the time, the likes of comedian Jimmy Carr and Celebrity Traitors star Joe Marler were connected with the presenting gig. Ramsay is a huge name. He has made tonnes of cooking shows in the UK and has had a wide ranging deal in the U.S. with Fox for years, fronting the likes of Hell’s Kitchen, Next Level Chef and Kitchen Nightmares . Last week, it was revealed he is rebooting Hell’s Kitchen for the UK’s ITV with Traitors host Claudia Winkleman and his production outfit Studio Ramsay Global. Ramsay said: “My love affair with cars began as a child, growing up a field away from Silverstone, where I would climb over the fences and sneak in for a glimpse of the racing. That early excitement sparked a lifelong passion for cars, motor sport, beautiful design and extraordinary engineering. At its very best Top Gear has always been about the unexpected – surprising, entertaining and just the right amount of chaos. That’s the spirit we want to build on, bringing a fresh energy and ambition to create something truly thrilling for a whole new generation of audiences.” Havard added that the rebooted offering will bring together “two iconic global powerhouses: the world’s most famous, high octane motor show and a car obsessed megastar.” “Gordon’s fierce and fearless approach makes him a natural fit, and we’re thrilled that audiences will see him in the driving seat as the show speeds into its next exciting era,” added Havard. Top Gear became a global phenomenon in the hands of Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond, James May and producer Andy Wilman. It enjoyed a second life when Chris Harris, Paddy McGuinness and Flintoff took over hosting duties from Matt LeBlanc and Chris Evans. Various versions of the show air around the world. An American Top Gear was made last decade first for the History Channel and then BBC America. Top Gear is produced by BBC Studios Entertainment Productions for BBC One and BBC iPlayer and was commissioned by Havard and Michael Jochnowitz, the BBC’s new Head of Constructed Reality and Studio Entertainment. For BBC Studios, the creative director is Mel Balac, the showrunner is Rowland French, and the executive producer is Zac Assemakis. title: How ‘The Other Bennet Sister’ Defied the Odds as a Smash Hit
full_text: Skip to main content By David Canfield Plus Icon David Canfield Senior Entertainment Writer View All November 25, 2026 9:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source In one of the most sweeping, romantic moments of The Other Bennet Sister , Tom Hayward (Dónal Finn) recites the poem “Composed Upon Westminster Bridge” for Mary Bennet (Ella Bruccoleri), Pride & Prejudice ‘s misfit sibling turned unlikely romantic heroine. The delivery of the poem is wrenching; the scene, in a small rainy garden, idyllic. And yet the scene, adapted by screenwriter Sarah Quintrell from Janice Hadlow’s novel of the same name, was scaled back dramatically from how it reads in the book — taking place against the splendor of the actual Westminster Bridge. Related Stories Lifestyle "Sometimes You Just Have to Think: 'What Will Make People Laugh?'": Lolly Adefope on Gags, 'Ghosts' and Her West End Debut TV NBC to Air Princess of Wales Cancer Charity Documentary “Our budget is a Mary-Bennet-[level], appropriate, ordinary, like-all-of-us sized budget — it’s not a kind of massive franchise genre-tastic kind of thing. It’s humble. We couldn’t film on Westminster Bridge — we just couldn’t afford it,” according to Emmy-winning executive producer Jane Tranter ( Succession ). “We were cramped into this tiny little garden full of rain…to create a scene that just feels so big and so moving and so emotional on very, very little. It’s all about text and performance and intent. That is what The Other Bennet Sister is all about. It’s not flashy or fancy, with loads of money spent on it. It’s about the truth and the emotion.” Audiences have taken note. It’s not just the full-house crowd that packed the San Vicente Bungalows on Friday evening to watch select clips from the series — and catch Tranter alongside Bruccoleri and Finn in conversation — as part of The Hollywood Reporter ’s exclusive THR Frontrunner screening series. Following its smash initial run in the U.K. on the BBC , The Other Bennet Sister drove unprecedented subscriber growth for North American distributor BritBox and generated wide critical acclaim. The 10-episode series will compete as a limited series this guild season as well as at next year’s Primetime Emmy Awards. A three-episode holiday special will air this Christmas. During the panel, the trio discussed key scenes from the original series before teasing the special to come. Dónal Finn and Ella Bruccoleri in The Other Bennet Sister. Bad Wolf/BBC/BritBox The show’s main attraction, of course, is Bruccoleri’s moving, nuanced turn, which embodies the core idea behind the show — that heroes on screen don’t always present the way we expect them to. “The dialogue seemed rooted in something that you didn’t see very often in period drama, where there were awkward overlaps and people saying something that wasn’t exactly what they wanted to say and kind of retracting it,” says the Wicker star of what appealed to her about the project. “I was really excited by seeing that on the page. It felt like I was reading a young woman that could have existed today, that could have existed at any time — and it just happened to be set in Regency England. But it felt really relevant to now.” The series centers on the romantic arc between Mary and Tom, who is engaged when they first meet; by the end of the finale, Tom and his previous fiancée have broken things off and he’s proposed to Mary. The special is set to explore the beauties and frustrations of their new marital life. “There’s a beautiful sentiment throughout The Other Bennet Sister , which is about examining societal norms and rules and what is expected of a young person or a young woman — how that narrative deserves to be examined and that there are opportunities in many ways to be happy,” Finn says. “[What] I love about these next three episodes is that there’s a further investigation of what it is to be happy in a relationship and to keep a hold of your individuality and to prioritize your systems of living and whether they serve you.” You can watch the full panel conversation above. The Other Bennet Sister is streaming on BritBox. THR
