title: Studio Lambert Is Digging Into The Archives For Its Next ‘Traitors’-Sized Hit
full_text: One of the interesting consequences of Banijay ’s merger with All3Media is that Stephen Lambert, who runs The Traitors producer Studio Lambert , has been reunited with his early work. Before Lambert, a former BBC documentary producer, founded Studio Lambert in 2008, he was Chief Creative Officer at RDF Media, where he produced series such as Wife Swap and Faking It. As a result of the merger, which values the company at around $8B, that brings together Banijay’s 130 production companies (including RDF Media, which was folded into Remarkable Entertainment in 2024) with All3Media’s 40 shingles, Lambert and his team, which includes Chief Creative Officer Tim Harcourt and U.S. President Jack Burgess, can now dig through his own archives in search of IP to plunder and shows to remake. Related Stories News ‘The Circle’ Moves To Hulu: Disney Streamer Orders New Version Of Studio Lambert Social Experiment News ‘Monopoly’: Studio Lambert Passes Go At Netflix After Winning Bake-Off For Reality Game Show Lambert told Deadline, “We’re excited to be part of a very big group. We’re excited about the fact that we have access to a pretty significant rights library, including a whole lot of shows that we did at RDF that we suddenly have access to.” Watch on Deadline Studio Lambert already has form bringing back and reinvigorating some of its biggest hits such as The Circle , which started life on Channel 4 in the UK, before becoming a Netflix series and is now streaming on Hulu, and Undercover Boss , which ran for 11 seasons on CBS between 2010 and 2022, and is now in production on a new season for the Skydance-owned broadcast network with Drew Carey as host. It will look to see whether there’s any new life for franchises such as Wife Swap , which was most recently turned into a Real Housewives vehicle, Faking It , the “modern-day Pygmalion” that ran for seven seasons in the UK and was adapted for TLC in the early noughties, Secret Millionaire , which was remade for both Fox and ABC between 2008 and 2012, and youth-skewing reality show Shipwrecked . “We’re going through it at the moment, trying to work out what we think is the best thing to do,” Lambert said. “There’s a wealth of opportunity and renaissance moments,” added Harcourt. The trio are aware that they are “a bit of an anomaly” within the broader Banijay group. “There hasn’t been quite enough clarity about the fact that we’re not in the country-specific setup. We’re not an American company working to the American system and we’re not a British company working to the British system,” said Lambert. “We’re a bit of an anomaly, but an anomaly that comes from the fact that we’re both British and American, and also we’re not fully owned by Banijay, so that makes quite a big difference as well.” They’re happy to be part of a big group, but they’re aware that “we hang and fall on our ability to come up with ideas and to sell shows and make them very well.” “It’s a new outlook for [the parent company], and so far everyone’s been very accommodating of our desire to keep working in the way that has been working for us,” added Burgess. They work closely with Jane Turton, the former All3Media CEO who is now Banijay’s Deputy CEO. Turton told Deadline, “Working with Stephen and Tim and the team at Studio Lambert is always exciting. The ideas, the shows, the success and, of course, the personalities are all big. Big bold ambitious ideas developed and produced to the very highest quality. It is a pleasure to be part of the Studio Lambert team and especially so now that we are part of the bigger Banijay Entertainment with its many production territories, deep IP catalogue and expertise in distribution, digital and live.” Unlike many transatlantic companies, Studio Lambert does not geo-block its ideas with key staff being incentivized to work on projects regardless of whether they land in the U.S. or UK. The Circle (Disney/Chuck Zlotnick) This was intentional to allow Studio Lambert entry into the “exclusive” club of producers that are trusted to make big shows. Lambert said that it started with The Circle , which was originally developed for Channel 4 in the UK before becoming a hit among younger viewers and being adapted for Netflix. “Our effort has been on these big, high-budget shows, which we knew that buyers, both in Britain and America, wanted. In this highly competitive market, [buyers] all know that they need these big, noisy tentpole shows. But they also know that if they order an idea and the people who are pitching it haven’t got the experience of making those very expensive shows, then it’s not just going to be a flop, it’s going to be their careers that are a flop for having ordered it. So, it does mean that they have to go with those people that have got the track record,” he added. The Circle led to The Traitors, which led to Squid Game: The Challenge , which led to Fallout Shelter: The Experiment. The company is currently in the middle of shooting The Circle for Hulu, which is streaming three episodes a week, hosted by Tinx and starring a mix of civilians and celebrities from Disney shows such as The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives, Vanderpump Villa and Dancing with the Stars. “It’s exciting, and fast turn as well. We’re making it one day, cutting it and then it’s on air 48 hours later,” said Harcourt. It was somewhat of a surprise that Hulu was able to land the rights, given that Netflix had premiered two seasons as recently as 2024. Burgess said that Hulu’s unscripted chief Rob Mills “jumped on the opportunity”. “There was a moment where he could he could do it, and they were instantly on board,” he said. “It was competitive as well,” added Harcourt. “There were other people that were that that were interested. It’s amazing that they’ve been able to do it.” Studio Lambert’s most buzzy show also features civilians and celebrities, albeit in separate versions. The Traitors (Euan Cherry/NBC) It has produced four seasons of The Traitors featuring civilians for the BBC, as well as an upcoming fifth one in 2027, and two celebrity versions. In the U.S., The Traitors: New Blood , featuring civilians, just wrapped its first season and was renewed for a second season by NBC , as well as four seasons of the celebrity version for Peacock and a fifth one coming next year. “A format is always best if it works with civilians because then you know it’s like waterproof,” said Harcourt. “The BBC One audience was never going to accept a bunch of celebrities running around in green cloaks so there [had] to be civilians. Then it success we can do it with celebrities.” “Conversely, in the U.S., having those tried and true reality stars who brought an audience was really helpful to us on Peacock. It was a platform that had Love Island , but didn’t have a ton of inventory there, and so you’re asking different questions of the audience, and it’s worked really nicely going the other way,” added Burgess. The Traitors has also been renewed for three further seasons, through season eight , by Peacock. “We’ve already interested our grandchildren. They want to know who’s going to be making the show in 2053,” joked Lambert. The trio paid tribute to Mike Cotton, who is the creative director of the franchise, and exec produces both the U.S. and UK series. They also believe there’s plenty of road for the format. “It’s still quite early in its life cycle. I’m sure if 27 years ago we were told that this little show Big Brother, that felt innovative, was still on the air everyone would have scoffed. It’s quite surprising how long the shelf life of IP actually is,” said Harcourt. In terms of big-budget competitions, the company is also passing go at Netflix with an adaptation of iconic board game Monopoly . Studio Lambert beat out around 50 rivals in a bake-off to land the right to produce the show , which has a $2M prize. It will see 12 contestants competing on a life-sized Monopoly board. “It’s a big world. We’ve brought the board to life, and we’ve taken the heart of the game, but changed it for television. I think the changes are brilliant,” said Lambert. “It turns out that a board game that every family ends up squabbling over makes for a really exciting reality game because those emotions are definitely brought to life in this game. Luckily, the board was too big for anyone to flip over,” added Burgess. Before it became one of the go-to producers for large-scale competition series, the feather in Studio Lambert’s cap was Undercover Boss. The show became a “great utility player” for CBS, which initially launched in behind the Super Bowl in 2010 and went on to air over 130 episodes. The Skydance-owned network revealed in September that it was bringing it back and, this time, with a host in Drew Carey. “Good shows never die, they just rest,” said Lambert. The first version of the show launched after the banking crisis and Lambert added that anxiety in the workplace and the American economy got CBS to the point where people would want to watch it again. “This season has been really fun because you realize just how different people’s work lives are now,” added Burgess. While the company prioritizes big-budget competitions, it has also struck a number of partnerships that allow it to play in different genres. These include launching Inner Drive Entertainment with Jon Barinholtz and Rob Belushi and bringing Vivian Choi and Jill Goslicky’s MindMeld Entertainment into the fold. MindMeld focuses on reality shows and docuseries with the pair having worked on Bravo’s Below Deck, while Inner Drive is game show focused. Burgess said that these teams bring different skill sets. MindMeld, for instance, may be able to take advantage of all of the reality stars that come through the Traitors universe. “I’m really excited about the stuff [these companies] have coming through,” he added. “It wasn’t that we thought we would help them make big shows like ours. It was more that we thought, let’s [have] our main creative effort concentrate on these big shows. But because we want to grow in all different ways, and we like working with great people, it’s a way of having different kinds of shows away from the main sort of thrust of what we’re doing and by having a relationship with them, we would hopefully help them get stuff away,” added Lambert. (L-R): Stephen Lambert, Jack Burgess, Tim Harcourt (Studio Lambert) The trio are confident that there are “tons of big opportunities in unscripted in the American market at the moment”. “I think we’re sort of at the end of a cycle of a glut of dramas that started in the pandemic and I think buyers see value in unscripted and the young large audiences that they can they can deliver,” said Harcourt. Every seven years or so, a new unscripted format emerges and becomes the lightning rod for others, which is exactly what The Traitors did. “What I hope that the takeaway from that will be is that something big and bold can still be a really big broad hit in unscripted. The focus for us isn’t what’s the next iteration of Traitors, it more what is the next big shape of a show that will be popular,” added Burgess. STUDIO LAMBERT SLATE: SQUID GAME: THE CHALLENGE The reality competition version of Netflix’s dystopian Korean hit is returning for a third season. This time, however, the show, which features a $4.56M prize, will feature celebrities alongside the civilian contestants. “It’s the VIPs versus the players with the jeopardy that the VIPs get sent to join the players when they fail. It’s great,” said Harcourt. THE MOB: Parker Posey moved into the treacherous world of reality competition with The Mob, which launched on Hulu in October. The series sent a group of celebrities, including The Mob will feature recognizable reality faces including The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives’ Demi Engemann and The Sopranos star Aida Turturro, to a lavish Italian villa where they shook down, hustled and whacked their way to win up to $250,000 in cash prizes. Burgess called it a “big bold world” and hopes that it returns for a second season. THE GOLDEN ELEVATORS: Studio Lambert has been working on a U.S. adaptation of the psychological quiz format, which was initially developed by John De Mol’s Talpa. The show, which has been piloted, sees ten contestants begin together in the lobby of a spectacular skyscraper with the aim of reaching the top floor and securing a $100,000 prize. It has already sold a UK version to ITV. “It’s got momentum,” said Burgess. RACE ACROSS THE WORLD: One of Studio Lambert’s most popular shows in the UK is Race Across The World, which has run for ten seasons including celebrity editions. The show does what it says on the tin, following pairs of competitors racing to reach a destination any which way other than air. Some believe it shares too much DNA with The Amazing Race to be remade in the States. Not Studio Lambert, however. “We’ve always believed that there’s a home for it in the U.S,” said Burgess. “Also, it doesn’t matter what the price of oil is on that show because you’re not allowed to take a flight, so it can survive that.” Read More About: Comments

title: “Sometimes You Just Have to Think: ‘What Will Make People Laugh?'”: Lolly Adefope on Gags, ‘Ghosts’ and Her West End Debut
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All November 25, 2026 8:33am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Lolly Adefope at the U.K. premiere of 'Ghosts: The Possession of Button House.' Courtesy of Getty If there’s one piece of advice Lolly Adefope wants to pass on to the next Mary Todd Lincoln, it’s from Broadway’s Maya Rudolph: Wear the kneepads. The British star has taken her undeniably brilliant comedy chops to the stage, making her West End debut in Oh, Mary! ‘s London transfer and joining a steadily growing — and deliciously mischievous — lineup of actors to take on the neglected wife of Abraham Lincoln at the Trafalgar Theatre (Catherine Tate, Mason Alexander Park, Jinkx Monsoon, as well as the show’s playwright Cole Escola among them). Related Stories Movies Ava DuVernay to Receive London Critics' Circle Inaugural Laura Mulvey Female Trailblazer Award Movies Damian Lewis Boards Short Film 'Odessa' as Executive Producer (Exclusive) The 80-minute musical, chronicling the days before the U.S. president’s assassination from the point of view of his alcoholic, cabaret-fanatic spouse, is a breathless romp with dance numbers, growling and some belt-out show tunes — all in a wig and corset. It took Adefope a couple of performances to realize it wasn’t do-or-die each night. “At first I was like, ‘This has to be all of my energy in every single second of the show,'” she begins to The Hollywood Reporter . “If you’re going to do one big show at Wembley Stadium, then yeah, you can let it all out. But it’s just not sustainable for the body to be under extreme tension for an hour-and-a-half. In the beginning, I was just kind of doing it like a panic attack. And then after a while I was like, ‘You can actually chill.'” It tracks that Adefope performs Oh, Mary! ‘s absurdity with the precision of a surgeon. She’s been described as the best part of everything she’s in — and it’s true. The South Londoner might be globally recognizable for roles in Hulu comedy Shrill or even the canceled-too-soon Franchise , but here in the U.K., she’s a titan of the British comedy circuit and possesses the kind of make-it-look-easy talent that some performers spend their entire careers searching for. Never is that more on display than in the BBC ‘s Ghosts , where Adefope ascertained household-name status with her scene-stealing portrayal of Kitty, an adorable Georgian noblewoman who also happens to be dead. “I think it came naturally to me,” says Adefope about character comedy and her early stand-up aspirations. “It was probably a good thing that I didn’t really have people in my life who were doing stand-up. It was all just a very class clown vibe, listening to lots of Radio 4 comedy, watching [comedy duo] Mitchell and Webb and absorbing comedy on Nickelodeon and Disney Channel.” It wasn’t until late into her teens that Adefope thought she could make a living out of it. “I had an idea that I wanted to be a comic actor,” she says, “but that felt like a made-up thing.” What does any young person with dreams of making a career out of cracking everyone else up do? Hit the Edinburgh Fringe Festival, of course. The must-stop for aspiring stand-ups and comedy performers has taken over the Scottish capital every August for 79 years, and served as a springboard for some of the most famous creatives in the business, such as Phoebe Waller-Bridge, Richard Gadd, Emma Thompson and Graham Norton. “It’s this one month where you get to live with all your friends and see your friends’ shows and when I was doing it, I was like, ‘I wish this was what real life was like!'” remembers Adefope. “Sadly, it’s not.” Lolly Adefope as Kitty and Jim Howick as Pat in ‘Ghosts.’ Courtesy of the BBC But it did land her an acting agent, and with that came one of her first paid gigs: Josh Widdicombe’s 2014 sitcom Josh . “The character’s name was Catherine or something. But in the beginning,” says Adefope, “it was called, like, ‘Annoying Girl at Party.’ And I was like, ‘Sign me up!'” The more she acted, the more Adefope believed she thrived in that space — particularly character work. It was on the game show Taskmaster and a slew of other now-non-existent British panel shows that her profile rose even higher. But it was a 2017 sitcom with Jim Howick, Loaded , that crucially got her acquainted with a member of theater collective Them There. “Jim called me and he was like, ‘We’re making this taster of this show. It’s called Ghosts ,'” she recalls. “‘Would you want to be in it?'” Them There, comprised of Howick, Mathew Baynton, Simon Farnaby, Martha Howe-Douglas, Laurence Rickard and Ben Willbond, raised a generation with the still meme-spawning series Horrible Histories , a sketch show depicting caricatured versions of England’s most prolific historical figures. They had a new pitch for the British broadcaster — a quasi-flat-share comedy in which a couple inherits an enormous stately home filled with the ghosts of those who spent time and died there throughout the centuries. Among the apparitions are a lightning-zapped caveman, a Regency-era poet shot in a duel, a boy scout counselor from the ’80s with an archery arrow through his neck, a victim of the Stuart era’s witch hunts, and a disgraced Tory minister who died mid-sex and is now destined to spend eternity without trousers on. Five seasons later, and Ghosts stands in pride of place in the U.K.’s comedy hall of fame. Its unprecedented success has made superstars out of its cast, hatched versions in the likes of the U.S., Germany, and France, and accrued a cool $11.2 million at the British box office with last month’s release of a feature film Ghosts: The Possession of Button House , reuniting the beloved characters after the show’s end in 2023. Since Katy Wix’s Mary ascended to a higher plane, or, as the ghosts say, got sucked off (“What can you do?” asks her former co-star with a faux pout), Adefope is the only performer who isn’t also a member of the writing team. She remains one of the show’s blindingly bright spots (of which there are many). “Kitty was pretty similar to how they first described her, but I think at first she was more stupid,” laughs Adefope about the initial conversations around her giggling, pop music-loving poltergeist. “But to this day, I’m like, ‘She’s the smartest ghost!’ I didn’t want it to be too two-dimensional — not that they would have ever written anything two-dimensional — but I am obsessed with Tituss Burgess [in Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt ] and Jack McBrayer in 30 Rock ; [the idea] that there’s something going on underneath the surface of this sweet character,” she says. Indeed, it’s in Adefope’s immediate understanding of the smartest possible decision — a sly eye roll, bashful giggle, or childlike outburst — that makes her work as Kitty so impressive. “I think a big chunk of it is probably wanting to make the rest of the guys laugh,” says the star about keeping the audience guessing with Kitty’s mannerisms. “Part of it is probably having a background in doing live comedy — it’s quite good training for that kind of show because there are loads of us, and you don’t get hours to do a take. Sometimes you do just have to think: ‘What is going to make people laugh? What’s the unexpected thing?'” She couldn’t have predicted the way the show would resonate with Brits. “It’s a very rare experience to make something that you love making and that people also love watching, because it’s sometimes one or the other,” says Adefope. But there certainly wasn’t any talk of a feature film after that fifth and final season wrapped up, or Adefope would have “really held onto that.” In the movie, the ghosts race to rescue a wandering spirit who’s possessed the body of a young boy before the child loses his life forever. “The writers always wanted to make sure that it wasn’t just a bonus, extra-long episode,” she says about the direction they took. “[They wanted it to feel] like it warranted being on a big screen, and it’s so nice having people watch and validate that. […] It does deserve to be longer and bigger.” She would admittedly do “100 sequels,” but the group is facing some major continuity hurdles. “The ghosts aren’t meant to age, and every year we all think we look older,” she laughs. “We don’t know how long we could do it for, but I don’t think there are any plans to do a sequel. But there were no plans to make any more after the TV show, so who can trust what they say?” Adefope is certainly well-acquainted with the false hope of a fickle entertainment business. The Franchise , HBO’s satirical superhero comedy from Jon Brown, Sam Mendes and Armando Iannucci, got the axe after one season (though it did also earn Adefope a BAFTA TV Award nomination). She repeats THR ‘s question with a knowing smirk: “Was it chopped down in its prime? It’s a great question. I was disappointed about The Franchise ,” she begins. “I think it was so funny when the trailer came out for The Studio and it was so similar to the show we were making. And it’s won the most Emmys of any comedy ever [now],” she says about the Seth Rogen-led Apple TV hit. “So did we stand a chance?” The question lingers. Lolly Adefope and Vinnie Heaven in the West End’s ‘Oh, Mary!’ Courtesy of Manuel Harlan Another U.S.-based project, Aidy Bryant’s three-season Shrill , would take Adefope to Portland every year for 12 weeks. “That definitely felt like, ‘Whoa, this is actor lifestyle vibes,'” she says about playing Bryant’s British best friend and flatmate, Fran. “I loved Shrill so much, it was a dream,” she continues. “[But] because I’d done a show before that called Miracle Workers in Atlanta, there was a period of time [and] even now people say, ‘Where are you living at the moment?’ I’m like, ‘I do actually live in London,’ but after that I [thought], ‘Maybe I should try and do some British work just so that people don’t think I’ve left.'” It might not get much more British than the West End, where Adefope has set up camp for the first time in Escola’s Tony Award-winning show. Its transfer has denied the naysayers here in London, extending its run and consistently pulling enormous audiences, including to Adefope’s slot, which wraps up Dec. 5. She saw the Broadway version — ”I was so giddy” — and immediately told Escola afterward that they should consider bringing it to London. It never occurred to Adefope that she could take on Mary Todd Lincoln herself. “I have never really known where to start in the theater world,” she muses. “But Oh, Mary! is just so my humor and it felt like my comic sensibilities matched it quite well. I let the phone ring,” she adds. “I didn’t beg for the audition myself,” a glimpse of Kitty emerges in those fluttering eyelashes, “because I was too shy.” It might not be a shock to hear that Adefope is an electrifying First Lady, imbuing her portrayal with the no-holds-barred cheekiness the character necessitates. As is the joy of Oh, Mary! , seeing her version is an entirely different experience compared to her predecessors’. Adefope’s Mary is uniquely her own. “I feel so lucky to be able to put my spin on something and for it to feel like it fits really well,” she says. “Sometimes you get a script for something and you’re like, ‘It doesn’t quite match with how I see the character.’ But this [was] an amazingly lucky fit that I felt I could inhabit it.” After agreeing to take on the role, the nerves followed soon after. “I had these weird thoughts,” confesses Adefope. “I was like, ‘I’m going to forget to go to the theater.’ And they’re going to be like, ‘Where is she?'” But those jitters were watered down when she remembered it’s already a beloved, award-winning show. (The only tough part now is a hard-to-please audience, “[or] if they’re quiet when I’m doing my manic, physical comedy.” It’s a rarity, she assures us.) Until December, Lolly Adefope has her kneepads on. “For the characters to get slightly further from myself is always fun,” she tells THR about what comes after. “I mean, Mary Todd Lincoln is quite far from myself, even though now I feel like she is me. But I’m doing lots of writing, and seeing where that goes, and [I’m] open to whatever comes next.” What that might entail is anyone’s guess, but one thing is for certain: this Ghosts alum will stay a pro at lifting spirits. THR

title: Sofia Carson, Taylor John Smith & Charlie Hall Board NFL Rom-Com ‘The Christmas Game’ From Netflix
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News 'Avengers: Doomsday' Tracking For All-Time Best $270M+ Opening Next Month; 'Dune 3' Eyes $75M+ Debut Read the full story By Matt Grobar Matt Grobar Senior Film Reporter More Stories By Matt Sofia Carson, Taylor John Smith & Charlie Hall Board NFL Rom-Com ‘The Christmas Game’ From Netflix Kevin Kline Joins Meryl Streep In Netflix’s ‘The Corrections’ Constance Wu, Macaulay Culkin, Ken Leung And Ethan Eng To Star In New A24 Film From Director Walter Woodman View All November 25, 2026 8:15am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Sofia Carson, Taylor John Smith, and Charlie Hall Elias Tahan/Kelsey Hale/Sergio Garcia EXCLUSIVE: Sofia Carson , star of such juggernaut Netflix rom-coms as My Oxford Year and The Life List , is set to star in The Christmas Game , a new NFL -themed holiday rom-com from the streamer. Up-and-comers Taylor John Smith ( Where the Crawdads Sing ) and Charlie Hall ( Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed ) complete the film’s love triangle. Directed by Laura Terruso , who helmed Netflix’s Sabrina Carpenter dance-crew comedy Work It , The Christmas Game revolves around a blunt, big-deal sports agent who is publicly dumped by her star client. She must then land an even bigger one to save her career — her NFL quarterback ex-boyfriend — before her rival signs him by Christmas. Related Stories News Netflix Only Big Player Not Funding UK's Independent Bullying & Harassment Complaints Body News Netflix As The New Cable: From Friend To Foe To Friend Again, How Streamer Became Go-To Source Of Off-Network Revenue & Tune-In Promotion Notably, The Christmas Game marks Netflix’s first narrative feature in partnership with the NFL and Skydance Sports Entertainment . While Christmas Day football has been a holiday staple at Netflix since 2024, the project brings that tradition onto the holiday movie slate for 2027. Watch on Deadline The script for The Christmas Game is by Danielle Morrow and Vanessa Marano, who previously penned the NFL rom-coms Holiday Touchdown: A Bills Love Story and A Make or Break Holiday for Hallmark Channel. Producers are Jesse Sisgold, Jason Reed and Sandino Moya Smith for Skydance Sports Entertainment. Carson and Jessica Matthews are exec producing. News of the film comes following a big first weekend for Guarding Stars , Netflix’s holiday rom-com starring Leighton Meester and Jared Padalecki, which racked up 27.6M views in its first three days. In addition to the projects aforementioned, Carson has found major success at Netflix with the romantic drama Purple Hearts , as well as Carry-On , the action-thriller from Jaume Collet-Serra, where she starred opposite Taron Egerton. The latter film is Netflix’s third most popular of all time, behind KPop Demon Hunters and Red Notice . The actress is repped by WME, Ziffren Brittenham and Kleinberg Lange Cuddy & Carlo. Previously seen in films such as Where the Crawdads Sing and Warfare , as well as HBO’s Sharp Objects , Smith is repped by CAA and Vybe Trybe. Hall stars opposite Tatiana Maslany in Apple’s acclaimed thriller Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed , heading into its second season. He’ll next be seen checking into The White Lotus Season 4 and is also set to write and star in a new college fraternity drug ring series, executive produced by Barry ‘s Alec Berg, for Netflix. He is repped by Untitled and CAA. Terruso most recently directed About My Father , the Lionsgate comedy starring Robert De Niro and Sebastian Maniscalco. She is repped by Verve and Artists First. title: All 17 Quentin Tarantino Movies, Ranked From Worst to Best
full_text: × Skip to main content From left: Brad Pitt in 'Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,' Samuel L. Jackson in 'Pulp Fiction' and Uma Thurman in 'Kill Bill' Courtesy Everett Collection (3) June, 1977. Cliff Booth runs the projector at the New Beverly Cinema, tends a couple bars, and drives a tow truck to a demolition derby. These are not his only day jobs, and they’re all at night. In his spare time, the ex-stuntman disappears blackmailers with a payoff or a bullet. Something called Star Wars has taken over theaters, threatening a half-century of blockbuster family fun. Cliff inhabits an older world, gnarly yet noble, gory and shagadelic. He runs with blaxploitation macks, bored Malibu wives, underworld assassins, the snobby former critic of the Superfood Gazette and whoever that body in the trunk used to be. These are Cliff Booth’s people — and Quentin Tarantino’s, too. Once upon a time in the 1990s, Tarantino was the breakout bad boy of independent film, surf riding the crest of a youth tsunami. Now he’s our reigning entertainer-historian, overstuffing hard-R sensations with motion picture lore. He owns the real New Beverly in actual Los Angeles. So when Netflix agreed to make his Once Upon a Time in Hollywood follow-up, they paid him a fortune to advertise his theater. Franchises have been no-brainers since, well, Star Wars . But a sequel on a streamer is something new for Tarantino. And The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth marks the first time in 30 years that someone besides him has directed one of his screenplays. Let’s get rambling to find out where it ranks in his filmography. 17. Past Midnight (1992) Image Credit: New Line Cinema/Courtesy Everett Collection He swears he will make only 10 films. We’re starting at 17. Is he lying, or is this list stupid? Probably both. However, this ranking seeks totality: his screenplays, his TV diversions, the simple fact that Kill Bill counts as two. Let’s count all his official writing and directing credits — plus this middling erotic thriller, which earned him a co-producer credit for doctoring the script. (He later polished Crimson Tide and The Rock .) A beautiful social worker with a bodacious lake house gets knocked up by an ex-con who maybe killed his pregnant wife. You hear trace Tarantino elements emerging in Past Midnight ’s dialogue, especially when a cop says the phrase “natural born killer.” And a very minor character, the snarky physician, is named “Dr. Zastoupil.” Quentin Tarantino was Quentin Zastoupil through childhood, keeping his stepfather’s surname even after his mom’s second divorce. A teen dropout with acting ambitions, he snagged “Tarantino” back from his biological father. Not because he loved the guy, matter fact he barely knew the son of a bitch. It just sounded better. 16. Four Rooms, “The Man From Hollywood” (1995) Image Credit: Claudette Barius/Miramax/Courtesy Everett Collection After Pulp Fiction won him his first Oscar, he hosted Saturday Night Live , got his head blown off in his buddy Robert Rodriguez’s Desperado , and played an animistic “god with a small g” named Johnny Destiny in the interminable Vegas comedy Destiny Turns on the Radio . Then came this dire anthology. Miramax must have hoped for generational showcase, with studio mascot Tarantino joining Rodriguez and their Sundance youngfriends Allison Anders and Alexandre Rockwell. Each filmmaker writes and directs their own New Year’s Eve farce, set on different floors on a Tinseltown hotel. Tarantino also stars in his entry, playing a fresh-minted shirtbird celebrity who complains if you call his Cristal mere champagne. It’s a wearisome (if admirably self-aware) snapshot of his peak overexposure, and a disastrous victory lap for the renegade age of indie cool. 15. My Best Friend’s Birthday (sometime in the 1980s) The rest of Four Rooms ’ band of outsiders started directing the regular independent way, with little money and amateur pluck. Anders’ and Rockwell’s first features were black-and-white cheapos about arty goofs, and Rodriguez wrote a book about El Mariachi ’s $7,000 budget. Reservoir Dogs looks insanely professional by comparison: soundtrack money, a prosthetic ear, Harvey Keitel. Tarantino’s missing link is this early unfinished comedy he directed about DJ pals on a manic night out. Acolytes peg My Best Friend’s Birthday as a True Romance beta test, though the fuzzy half-hour cut online suggests an alternate timeline where he made loosey autobiographical romcoms instead of meticulous profane epics. Pompadoured with earrings like some rockabilly nerdpunk, his character plainly admits he has a foot fetish. 14.75. CSI: Crime Scene Investigation , “Grave Danger — Volumes 1 and 2” (May 19, 2005) Image Credit: Robert Voets/CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images He owns a couple theaters, co-hosts a movie podcast, and wrote a great book of film criticism. Still, deep down, I wonder if Quentin Tarantino is more of a TV guy. His work chases an old forever feeling of channel-surfing into some random weekly episode about characters walking from place to place, meeting people, and getting into adventures. In the 1996 biography King Pulp , author Paul A. Woods memorably quotes Steve Buscemi: “When I saw Pulp Fiction , the little boy watching this big TV, being alone in the room, the TV being his friend — to me, that’s Quentin.” Does that explain why, fresh off Kill Bill ’s impressive exertion, he directed a couple hours of a hit procedural he adored? Wiliam Petersen’s brainiac cop Gil Grissom reveals an abiding fandom for Roy Rogers. Frank Gorshin and Tony Curtis play themselves. George Eads’ niceguy Nick hallucinates his own autopsy while buried alive. 14.5. ER , “Motherhood” (May 11, 1995) Image Credit: Chris Haston/NBCU Photo Bank/Getty Images CSI was already half-lame by 2005. This NBC hospital drama was still blazingly cool in its first season. And while Tarantino dutifully hits CSI ’s CBS marks, he brings an exuberant kick (and some cool long takes) to ER ’s Mother’s Day episode. One patient is newly earless. Julianna Margulies and Sherry Stringfield lay out on the roof, barefoot and sunglassed. 14.25. The best scene in Sin City (2005) Image Credit: Dimension Films/Courtesy Everett Collection For one cultural millisecond, in the month between the third El Mariachi and the first Kill Bill , Rodriguez was awesomer than Tarantino. Actually, he came off like the real Tarantino: a legitimate peddler of anything-for-a-dollar gut thrills, not a devoted student expostulating the genre curriculum. Alas, Rodriguez early-adopted all the millennium’s annoying industry trends: 3D, CGI backlots, HiDef video, rigid adherence to sacred Comic-Con texts. A lot of hot shit gets fucked in his frantic adaptation of Frank Miller’s comic noir. The ensemble shot in a void; post-production filled in the cartoon cityscape. Tarantino was “Special Guest Director” for helming practically the only sequence without violence, when Clive Owen’s heroic goon drives Benicio Del Toro’s evil goon to the local tar pits. Del Toro’s already dead, which doesn’t stop him from having a very entertaining conversation. Easy to guess this greenscreen pit of hell was not Tarantino’s bag. He kept filming on film, and made celluloid his theaters’ mission statement. 14. Kill Bill: Vol 1 (2003) and 13. Natural Born Killers (1994) Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection (2) Movies! Good for you, or bad? The first Kill Bill ornated Uma Thurman’s vengeance quest with samurai codes, Ennio Morricone needle drops, Shaw Brothers zooms, weeks of wirework, and fountains of bloodgush. When martial arts legend Sonny Chiba rhapsodizes about the sword he just made, it’s sheer religious ecstasy for a cultural obsessive. A decade earlier, director Oliver Stone adapted an early Tarantino screenplay into a screed against media obsession. Woody Harrelson and Juliette Lewis play Bonnie and Clyde plus MTV, sinners idolized into celebrities by our broken culture. Acclaimed cinematographer and psychedelic wizard Robert Richardson shot both Kill and Killers , blending multiple stocks and intense aesthetics. You don’t watch these films. You inhale. To the straight world of 1994, Tarantino and Stone probably looked like identical madmen. There was no love lost. Tarantino disavowed Stone’s Killers and published his original script as a middle finger. Stone added activist Russell Means as a kind of shaman, declaring with moral authority that the whole problem is “too much TV.” I assume Tarantino thought Stone was a preachy boomer, and that Stone saw Tarantino as everything wrong with a Generation X. Who was right? Are we living in a dark dystopia of true-crime infotainment and mass-transmitted megalomania? Or a wonderworld of multicultural exchange, with no divisions between highbrow and lowbrow, where a “silly Caucasian girl” in Bruce Lee’s clothes becomes a feminist action hero? Actually, they both nailed it. And these Kill fests only rank so low because I’m an old man who prefers 20-minute dialogues to 20-minute action scenes. 12. From Dusk Till Dawn (1996) Image Credit: Dimension Films/Courtesy Everett Collection Rodriguez directed and Tarantino wrote this genre mash-up. The divide between their styles is clear as the Tex-Mex border. Dusk ’s daylit first hour is pure rancid QT-inflected neo-noir. George Clooney — never meaner, never hotter — and Tarantino himself play the fugitive Gecko Brothers. Killers fatale Juliette Lewis and top Reservoir dog Harvey Keitel are RV-riding normals forced to drive the bros south to El Rey. Oddly, the fun falls off at the halfway twist, when surprise vampires lock the doors at the Titty Twister and trap the cast in a horror-comedy. Still, the closing lines pinpoint Tarantino’s unsteady moral code. “I may be a bastard,” says the last man standing, “But I’m not a fucking bastard.” 11. Grindhouse (2007) Image Credit: Weinstein Company LLC/Courtesy Everett Collection From Dusk Till Dawn also has the snake dance: Salma Hayek, wearing little except a Burmese python, pouring liquor down her leg so Tarantino can drink it off her toes. An astonishing scene, really, if you only care about desire. When he directs, Tarantino is comparatively chaste. He prefers a good flirt, with comfortable silences. He’s only filmed one sex scene — in Jackie Brown , in the kitchen, standing, 9/10ths clothed, loveless — unless you count a couple man-to-man assaults. I’m talking about sex because Grindhouse , the flop that ended his Rodriguez partnership, turned into their big sex movie: gauzy with the male gaze, an essential artifact from the dirtbag 2000s. They each made their own film, then released them together as a three-hour double-bill. (Never watch the split-off versions. For better and worse, the three-hour experience depends on too-muchness.) Rodriguez’s kickoff feature, Planet Terror , is the more obvious HR nightmare: Produced by then-wife Elizabeth Avellán, starring eventual girlfriend Rose McGowan as a gun-legged go-go dancer, overseen by the studio boss who wound up disgraced for assaulting multiple women (including, allegedly, McGowan.) Tarantino’s Death Proof is smarter and safer, punctuating all-female convos with car-assaults by Kurt Russell’s ladykiller stuntman. The director later told the Church of Tarantino podcast that he based Tracie Thoms’ badass driver on a girlfriend and all the women onscreen reflect genuine female posses he rolled with. I dunno. The chicks’ habits mostly evoke novelist Gillian Flynn’s immortal line that “Cool Girls are above all hot.” Lotta booze-swilling daisy-duked dames here, who dig Zatoichi and keep finding new ways to put their feet up. You can’t be cynical when the climax is an act of friend-to-friend hero worship. Stuntwoman Zoë Bell was Thurman’s Kill Bill stunt double. Fascinated by her talent — and furious at the computers invading fast cinema — Tarantino cast Bell as herself to ride on top a Dodge Challenger for an all-time car chase. In her daffy stunt-action charisma, you spot the primordial Cliff Booth: genial, lusty for danger, more than a little insane. 10. Django Unchained (2012) Image Credit: Andrew Cooper/Weinstein Company/Courtesy Everett Collection Since we’ve talked about sex, we should talk about race. Spike Lee was not the only one noticing all the n-words in Tarantino’s dialogue. To love his work, you do have to kinda think cultural appropriation is a good thing, that it’s okay for anyone — even a white kid from the South Bay — to melt the cultures he adores into one big pot. That may even be the conventional wisdom; Tarantino’s biggest success is his Blackest. Jamie Foxx stars as the freedman learning the bounty trade from Christoph Waltz’s cheerful German. Tarantino won his second Oscar for a baggy script, which runs an hour longer than Sergio Corbucci’s stupendously garish Django (source of Unchained ’s name and theme song). Foxx’s gunslinger is too mythic for any personality, especially compared to Leonardo DiCaprio’s plantation tyrant Calvin Candie. But Tarantino has always been interested in performance as an act of self-preservation. (Track how many people on this list go deep undercover into a life-or-death con.) Foxx comes alive when Django playacts race betrayal as a Black slaver. As the head of Candie’s household, Samuel L. Jackson gives what amounts to a ferocious double role, plotting brilliantly behind a mask of loudmouth servitude. 9. Kill Bill: Vol 2 (2004) Image Credit: Miramax/Courtesy Everett Collection After the Crazy 88 fight wraps the first volume on an operatic high, the deadliest woman in the world gets taken down by… Budd, a drunk with a shotgun. Tarantino regular Michael Madsen plays the ruminative assassin as the one person in the Bill ogy who lives anywhere close to reality. Working in an empty strip club and living alone in the desert, Budd is another proto-Cliff, a doomed killer basking in the slushy margarita of his decay. 2 is great fun — the showdown in Budd’s trailer is Tarantino’s best fight, period — until the talky finale veers baffling. Despite Thurman’s all-in performance, I’m not sure she (or anyone) can fully unpack the romantic-paternal Bill-Bride dynamic. Was the anticlimax purposeful? After months of martial arts training, David Carradine’s one big bit of choreography is a 12-second seated swordfight. Tarantino used to promise a third volume, possibly suspecting that 2 ’s happy ending left unfinished business. 8. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (2026) Image Credit: Courtesy of Netflix I love it. I love it! You’re telling me David Fincher — the serious man, the hundred-take cyborg, the serial killer fetishist — you’re telling me that David Fincher directed a plotless meander about a dude in puka shells bopping around Los Angeles? Cliff Booth looks fuzzier than Once Upon a Time in Hollywood , because digital still can’t capture night like 35mm. The obvious CGI (and alleged AI) adds to the cut-rate effect — like some high-tech toupee the whole screen is wearing. With Leonardo DiCaprio’s sadsack Rick gone, Pitt’s good-timer Cliff mixes banana margaritas, plays tennis, watches TV with his pops, and walks the earth like Caine in Kung Fu . “I’m not that deep,” he tells Elizabeth Debicki’s tall drink of Aussie. Co-star Yahya Abdul-Mateen II has a specific line, “This don’t mean shit to me,” that gets repeated a couple times. Should we trust that carefree attitude? Is this Tarantino’s Walking Tall Part 2 , a low-ambition cruise backward through pleasurable familiar territory? Don’t miss the elegiac resonance. Cliff’s a gig-economy freelancer juggling six or seven jobs, scamming friends out of cash, commodifying his own buff bod, living with a gainfully employed parent. The biggest movie of 1977 is about to bankroll the rise of Industrial Light & Magic, which will do for stuntmen what ChatGPT is about to do to me. From that perspective, Cliff’s commitment to joy isn’t just infectious. Motherfucker, it’s revolutionary. ( Read The Hollywood Reporter ’s full review here .) 7. Reservoir Dogs (1992) Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection Still his cleanest screenplay, especially when things get messy. A wild bunch of color-coded badmen congregate in a safehouse. Somebody’s dying, somebody’s lying, somebody’s crazy, and everyone’s armed. Skeptics noted similarities to Ringo Lam’s City on Fire . That Chow Yun-Fat thriller has romance, impressive heists, and a sincere cop-criminal friendship. Dogs ’ robbery is unseen. The one woman is a doomed bystander. The most tender friendship aims toward oblivion. What a cast: Keitel’s gruff Mr. White, Madsen’s smirkish Mr. Blonde, Tim Roth’s gutshot Mr. Orange. Even pallid quirkster Steve Buscemi looks damn slick as Mr. Pink, nailing Tarantino’s caffeinated patter and the perfect SoCal deployment of “man” as a punctuation mark. Buscemi should have been in all these movies. At a minimum, he should have played any part Tarantino wrote for himself. 6. The Hateful Eight (2015) Image Credit: Andrew Cooper/The Weinstein Company/Courtesy Everett Collection Skeptics call him ironic or nihilistic, but Tarantino does believe in good guys. The Bride, Cliff Booth, Django, and even Zoë Bell are paragons, their violence justified by righteous vengeance. Django appeared in the original concept of this snowblood frontier mystery, until Tarantino realized his white hell had no place for an iconic moral compass. Django became Major Marquis Warren, plantation-raised Union veteran, brilliant sleuth, unrepentant killer, documented Friend of Lincoln — and the greatest Tarantino character, played by the greatest actor to ever spout a Tarantino monologue. What secret does Samuel L. Jackson understand about his longtime director? Is it just a Tennessee thing: One born in Nashville, the other raised in Chattanooga? Hateful Eight traps Jackson’s disgraced veteran in a stagecoach stop with seven other tough customers. Three hours in a blizzard would feel claustrophobic, if everybody wasn’t such a riot. Kurt Russell’s noose-happy bounty hunter comes off crude and naïve. Jennifer Jason Leigh’s captive looks on, watchful and feral. Walton Goggins chatters memorably as the jerky bigot who worships a Confederate husk played by Bruce Dern. At once statelier and more bugfuck than Django , this second Western of Racism luxuriates toward its nutty-in-ever-sense twist. Make of this what you will: In the High Obama days of liberal goodwill, Tarantino made three features looking back (and ahead) toward fascism and white supremacy. 5. True Romance (1993) Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection Yes, Christian Slater is too pretty as Clarence, a Sonny Chiba-worshipping Quentinian comics clerk. Yes, the dark nonlinear screenplay got straightened out with a happy ending. Yes, the score has a lotta marimba. No, I don’t believe a sweet call girl like Patricia Arquette’s Alabama would ever fall for a geeky john her fourth day on the job. Director Tony Scott saw something in Tarantino’s writing, though, that nobody else ever found. Met-cute and insta-wed, Clarence and Alabama flee smoky Detroit for sunny California, with stolen coke in their bag and hell following after them. Gary Oldman, Christopher Walken, and James Gandolfini are all memorable baddies, even more impressive since they all only have a scene or two. A couple detectives come off like lunatics, because they’re played by Tom Sizemore and Chris Penn, men never known for their good behavior. It all works as glossy gutter pulp, set with comic precision in the chlorinated motels and rollercoasters of Los Angeles. But Scott was a true romantic. He makes Alabama and Clarence the greatest of Tarantino’s straightforward heroes, so stupid with passion that even colliding criminal underworlds can’t stop their love. Sound like a fairy tale? Fine. Pretend it’s called Once Upon a Time in Hollywood . 4. Inglourious Basterds (2009) Image Credit: Weinstein Company/Courtesy Everett Collection 1978’s The Inglorious Bastards was a rude romp about semi-psychotic soldiers in Occupied France. That’s the sort of squad-on-a-mission plot Brad Pitt’s Aldo Raine seems to be arranging in this similar-titled war film. The Lieutenant assembles eight Jewish servicemen (and one Hugo Stiglitz) to scalp a hundred Nazis apiece. But Aldo and his Basterds only show up after a lengthy opening interrogation, which introduces Waltz’s Jew-hunting Hans Landa. Then the Americans mostly disappear for a whole middle hour. The action shifts to a Paris cinema, and a basement bar. Parallel plots converge. Mélanie Laurent’s moviehouse operator seeks revenge for her murdered family. Aldo and his allies devise an attack. Goebbels (that Goebbels) hopes Der Führer (dat Führer) loves his new movie. Basterds ’ tavern setpiece marked a complete inversion from Kill Bill ’s excess: Twenty dialogue-heavy minutes of twisted-nerve tension followed by 15 onslaught seconds. It’s the Inglourious experience in micro, full of vivid characters and fatal consequences. 3. Jackie Brown (1997) Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection After Pulp Fiction , everyone knew what “Tarantinoesque” meant: Funny, shocking, loquacious, retro, now. Then he returned with a marvelous, middle-aged, low-key caper about a desperate flight attendant and a bail bondsman sick of bonding bails. “Didn’t exactly set the world on fire, did you, Jackie?” a lout detective teases the title character, who makes a piddling $16,000 plus benefits before she gets popped smuggling cash with a sprinkle of cocaine. Tarantino was casting Pam Grier for talent, not just stuntcasting her ‘70s fireball persona. When Jackie lands in jail, the soundtrack cranks the song Grier sang for the 1971 prison-hottie wackfest The Big Doll House — but the look on her face tells you the wild days were a long time ago. She finds an unlikely ally in Robert Forster’s Max Cherry, a bond agent weathered by years of scum and bureaucracy. Jackie’s big problem (and biggest opportunity) is Ordell Robbie, a gun dealer astounded at his own cleverness. Add in Robert De Niro’s semi-verbal ex-con and Bridget Fonda’s pothead siren, and you’ve got a collection of misfits in the South Bay — the former home of Quentin Zastoupil. Jackie Brown is the director at his least Tarantinoesque and most Zastoupilian, uncovering surprising soul in a landscape of food courts, airplane-hotel bars, beach pads, delusional small time crooks, and the occasional oil derrick. Transplanting Elmore Leonard’s novel from Miami, Tarantino chopped a gunfight, unrequited the romance, turned a white woman Black — and added one last ambiguous kiss. 2. Pulp Fiction (1994) Image Credit: Miramax Films/Courtesy Everett Collection What’s your favorite chapter? The buzz in ‘94 fixated on Vincent Vega and Mia Wallace at Jack Rabbit Slim’s, that binary-star supernova of John Travolta’s comeback and Uma Thurman’s arrival. Me and my teen buddies, scared or baffled by love, preferred the middle segment, with a katana-wielding Bruce Willis. The final act of corpse disposal has the most questionable rep, depending whether you think Tarantino’s acting is serviceable or unforgivable. (He’s fine.) Yet it’s the last bit that reveals Jackson’s Jules Winnfield as Pulp ’s moral core. Tarantino characters rarely change in the screenwriting-101 sense — he keeps casting Brad Pitt to specifically not do an emotional arc — but Jules is transformed after six point-blank bullets miraculously don’t execute him. In a moment of clarity, he starts wondering over Ezekiel 25:17, the Bible verse he’s been misquoting. Has he been his brother’s keeper? Or the tyranny of evil men? Heavy themes for a sensational quotefest, but Tarantino was always after more than his bratty referential imitators. His characters dress cool, talk cool, murder cool, and know cool things. It’s not enough to just be cool. So Jules becomes a killer who doesn’t kill — a Bad Mother Fucker trying real hard to be the shepherd. 1. Once Upon a Time in Hollywood (2019) Image Credit: Andrew Cooper/Columbia Pictures/Courtesy Everett Collection Brad Pitt exudes folkloric chill as convertible cowboy Cliff Booth. Whereas Leonardo DiCaprio’s Rick Dalton is all hat and no cattle, a whiskey-soured mess with a nervous stutter. They’re near-nobodies in Hollywood ’s Hollywood: A stuntman who can’t get stunt jobs, a fading TV star clutching guest parts. One memorable day, they both go to different fake Wests. Rick’s on a backlot doing a cowboy TV pilot. Cliff returns to the defunct western town at Spahn Ranch, where lurks doom. A fatal mood lingers, even if you don’t know the history. Rick got famous on Bounty Law for never bringing back his targets alive. Cliff maybe-definitely killed his wife. Zoë Bell is the stuntlady who refuses to work with a spouse-killer — hilarious, since Kurt Russell plays her stuntman husband, and they were the stuntpeople trying to kill each other four movies ago. That’s just one way Tarantino Voltrons together his whole filmography into his magnum opus. Here’s a Los Angeles thriller, a meta-western, and an alternate history, with Grindhouse -worthy re-enactments and a whole society incapable of turning off the radio or the television. There’s even — call Oliver Stone! — a meditation on screen violence, with one wannabe murderer declaring “If you grew up watching TV, that means you grew up watching murder!” Is it weird the heroes are older men, while the Mansonites (Margaret Qualley, Sydney Sweeney, Mikey Madison, Austin Butler, Maya Hawke) turned out to be Gen Z’s top stars this decade? I think Tarantino was being honest about late midlife fears, with Rick in particular worrying that some whole rising generation of longhairs is coming for his ass. There’s always been so much you don’t see in Tarantino’s movies, though, like Dogs ’ jewelry store or Pulp ’s briefcase. The climactic awe in Hollywood is how magnificently one big nothing happens. Margot Robbie’s Sharon Tate is a luminous mystery, worshipped yet unknowable. Manson himself barely appears. Tarantino resurrects an era that finished horrifically in the true 1969, then merrily twists the facts. Sadness embeds in that fantasy. We know the end came and will come again. Celluloid projection won’t return to the global multiplex, no matter how many repertory theaters Tarantino runs. Nobody lasts forever, in Hollywood or anywhere else. Good thing art is death proof. THR

title: ‘The Trip To The Northern Lights’: IFC Acquires Latest In Michael Winterbottom, Steve Coogan & Rob Brydon Franchise

An April 9, 2027 theatrical release has been set. IFC has been the home of the previous four chapters in The Trip series which has spanned the duo’s journeys throughout the UK, Italy, Spain and Greece. More than five years since their Grecian escapades, 2x Oscar nominee Coogan and 5x BAFTA Award nominee Rob Brydon reunite to tour the rugged beauty of northern Europe. What follows is a trek through Scandinavia in search of fine food, wry conversation and a glimpse of the elusive Northern Lights. The duo soak up northern Europe’s wildest reaches, from sculptural Swedish hotels to remote Norwegian islands in what is equal parts travelogue and midlife reckoning. They have been brilliant partners ever since the first Trip all those years ago. The Trip to the Northern Lights takes Steve and Rob from Malmo in southern Sweden through Norway’s spectacular fjords to the Lofoten Islands in Norway’s Arctic circle. I hope the audience enjoys the journey as much as we did.” Watch on Deadline “The Independent Film Company is thrilled to continue our longstanding relationship with this world-class group of filmmakers on the latest installment of this beloved franchise. Few comedic partnerships have the enduring appeal of Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon, and under Michael Winterbottom’s inspired direction, each new trip remains the comedic gift that keeps on giving. This time around, we can’t wait for audiences to join us on the road to the Northern Lights,” said Ayo Kepher-Maat, Independent Film Company’s Acquisitions and Production VP. “Michael Winterbottom, Steve Coogan and Rob Brydon have created a franchise filled with taste, wit and belly laughs. Independent Film Company has brought each one to audiences with characteristic care and capability. The Trip to the Northern Lights advances the history with the delight of something completely fresh and tasty,” said Josh Sapan of Sapan Studio. The Trip to the Northern Lights is produced by Melissa Parmenter and Josh Hyams for Revolution Films. The deal was negotiated by Ayo Kepher-Maat on behalf of Independent Film Company and Tristan Whalley MD of Goalpost Films on behalf of the filmmakers. title: ‘Clashing Through the Snow’ Director Carlson Young on Going From “Horror Girly” to Holiday Rom-Com
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lexy Perez Plus Icon Lexy Perez Senior Digital Editor and Producer View All November 25, 2026 7:45am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Carlson Young Nick Rasmussen Near the end of Clashing Through the Snow , Michelle Randolph ‘s Hannah Hendricks walks past an Eloise portrait in a New York hotel lobby. Standing beside it, holding her then seven-month-old daughter, is the film’s director, Carlson Young . “It really choked me up, even as I was walking through the shot,” Young tells The Hollywood Reporter. The moment felt “spiritually correct” for the rising director, who recalls dressing as Kay Thompson’s Eloise for her fourth-grade book day. Filming it with her baby on her hip gave her “this kind of out-of-body experience, overlapping-reality thing” that she felt “a lot of little girls could relate to.” Related Stories TV How Amin Joseph Brought "Humanity" to Sonny Liston in 'The Greatest' TV How 'Landman' Star Michelle Randolph Found Love ... In a Rental Car It’s a heartwarming moment in a heartwarming movie, and perhaps a surprising film for a director who calls herself a “horror girly.” Before moving behind the camera, Young built her career as an actor, with credits including Key & Peele , a guest role on Netflix’s Emily in Paris and the 2014 comedy Premature . Her breakout came as Brooke Maddox on MTV’s Scream , the 2015 TV series adaptation of the horror film franchise created by Kevin Williamson and directed by Wes Craven, and Young credits the horror genre with making her want to tell stories in the first place. “When I was a little girl, horror got me out of bed in the morning. Those are the directors I watched as a kid that made me want to be a director and a storyteller.” Having worked with “incredible horror directors on Scream ,” Young became fascinated by “what fear has to teach us,” and that curiosity guides her work as a director, even in romance. Her horror “sensibility and natural instinct,” she says, allow her to “clearly identify, in any given scene, where the psychic predator actually is.” Years later, Young has directed Prime Video ‘s new cozy holiday rom-com, with snowstorms, rental cars, a bus full of elderly passenger, bookstores and enemies-to-lovers banter, and she says those horror instincts and her love for nostalgic romances are exactly what helped her find its heart. “I didn’t necessarily think my next movie would be a holiday rom-com, but I fell in love with the script,” she tells THR . “It reminded me of so many classic holiday rom-coms that I’m nostalgic for.” Clashing Through the Snow , which debuted on Prime Video on Monday, stars Landman’ s Michelle Randolph and The Summer I Turned Pretty breakout Chris Briney as Hannah Hendricks and Ryan Mitchell, rival book editors competing for a career-saving publishing deal. When their flight is canceled, the pair are forced to share a rental car to New York City in the middle of a holiday snowstorm, each determined to close the deal first. And of course chaos ensues with the holiday journey anything but jolly. “It’s a comedy of errors, hijinks ensue, it’s a very fun movie, but it does have something to say as well,” Young say of Clashing Through the Snow (pictured on set with Randolph). Prime Video The film, which can also serve as a love letter to books and reading, was pitched as a Planes, Trains and Automobiles for a new generation, a comparison Young says she had to shed “right off the bat” or risk being overwhelmed by anxiety. Still, she found her film’s driving force in the heart of the 1987 road-trip comedy: the moment John Candy’s Del Griffith tells Steve Martin’s Neal Page, “I like me.” In Clashing Through the Snow , that heart comes in a vulnerable motel-room conversation in which Ryan tells Hannah she’s “living a when-then life.” The line spoke personally to Young and became the foundation for the film’s long, funny and often chaotic journey. “It resonated with me deeply, and I felt like it’s in the zeitgeist. So yes, it’s a comedy of errors, hijinks ensue, it’s a very fun movie, but it does have something to say as well,” Young says. “I did try to do our own version — pay homage to the classic holiday movies that we come back to every year and try to do something new.” Clashing Through the Snow may be her newest film, but it also marks a milestone for the director, who kept a “when-then” promise of her own. “I told myself, ‘When I direct three movies, then I can have a baby.’ And that’s actually what happened,” she says. “It’s really cool to bring my daughter into a world where I’m able to do what I’m passionate about and have her by my side. What could be more beautiful than that?” *** Young was on the sunny beaches of Mallorca, Spain, wrapping production on Prime Video’s romantic drama The Last Sunrise when she set her sights on Clashing . She would trade a sun-soaked summer romance for a snowy, cross-country road trip that takes place during the holiday season. And though she was already attached to direct, she still needed the right home for it. She had already worked with Amazon on the 2024 romance Upgraded , starring Camila Mendes, and on The Last Sunrise , with Maia Reffico, Fernando Lindez and Eva Longoria, which was then still forthcoming (it debuted in July 2026). For Clashing , her third film with Amazon, she again found a partner in the streamer. “It made sense, and it’s a movie I really believed in and knew would be great there with the team at Amazon,” Young says of bringing the film to Prime Video. With two films out on Prime Video this year, Young has come a long way from her directorial debut, the short film The Blazing World , which premiered at the 2018 Sundance Film Festival. Since then she has directed the 2021 feature-length version of The Blazing World ; Upgraded , which has a confirmed sequel; and the survival thriller Trust , starring Sophie Turner. From left: Young and Santiago Segura in Scream: The TV Series. Eliza Morse/MTV/Everett And while her turn as fan favorite Brooke Maddox in MTV’s iteration of the iconic horror franchise catered to her love for horror, Clashing and its exploration of “living a when-then life” made for a personal, art-imitating-life moment for the director. “I catch myself in that pattern almost constantly — this natural withholding of, ‘I have to accomplish this before I can give myself this.’ I think that’s very reflective of the world we live in, with the overstimulation and the high speed. We live in overdrive, so it’s something I deal with in real time,” she says. “From a career perspective, I hope to be able to look back at the end of my life and feel meaning in the work I’ve done. I try really hard with every movie I direct to weave in the medicine I’m capable of reflecting at the time.” *** Young with Camila Mendes on set of Upgraded . Paul Stephenson /© Amazon Prime Video / Courtesy Everett Collection With The Last Sunrise and now Clashing Through the Snow, the films have marked breakout moments for their leading stars. The Last Sunrise marked Lindez’s first English-language role, while Clashing is Randolph and Briney’s first foray as leading rom-com stars. Having come up as an actor first, Young has found a kinship in directing talent amid these moments in their journey. “I understand how vulnerable it is to be an actor. I think that’s a really important thing for directors to be sensitive to — and to know that actors also have incredible ideas. So I love to let whoever I’m working with play, and having been an actress first informs so much of what I do.” And how does acting inform her directing? She approaches it from a “different altitude.” “I don’t read a script anymore and think, ‘Oh wow, I’d really like to play this character.’ I read a script now with this bird’s-eye view. I feel much more spider-like, weaving different stories and characters together. But I’m actor-first, character-first, so it informs every decision I make as a director.” Briney is a talent she predicts “has a long career ahead of him, with many places to go and explore.” “I felt like seeing him in a more comedic role would be something incredibly fresh for him. When I met him and spoke to him, it was very obvious that he could do that, so I was really excited to find this character with him. He’s a very charming human, and he’s kind and resourceful. We got to have a lot of fun on set — I would just pitch him jokes and he would land them. He has a real comedic flexibility that I think is super fresh in his generation of actors,” she says. As for Randolph, Young was struck by the “charm and warmth that she exudes.” “She just has this effortless charm of the ’90s and 2000s rom-coms that I think we’re all so nostalgic for.” Young says of pairing them, “They’re both incredibly charming and talented actors in their own right, so it’s a dream to put those two together.” Christopher Briney and Randolph in Clashing Through the Snow. Brian Douglas / © Amazon MGM Studios / Courtesy Everett Collection In addition to Briney and Randolph, the film features a host of familiar faces, including Julia Fox, Andrew Schulz, Lucas Gage, Jake Shane, Tan France, Zarna Garg and even Paris Hilton. Young laughs when it’s suggested the internet showed up for the road trip. “You took the words right out of my mouth. The internet is showing up for this road trip,” she says. “This movie is for the chronically online.” Each brought the kind of levity the story needed, she says, and the known faces give the audience a familiarity “that feels like a warm hug. You kind of know this person; you’re aware of the energy they bring. It was a really fun recipe. It’s like a cake of the internet.” As for Hilton, who shares a comedic exchange with Briney’s Ryan at one point in the film, Young explains that the randomness of her guest role made the rivalry between Ryan and Hannah even more fun. “We were like, who is a person Ryan could interface with at the Bianca Hart show who would make Hannah go, ‘How the fuck do you — what is going on here?’ She’s so iconic in her own right, and picturing her in that moment made me laugh out loud.” *** Teasing “a lot of exciting projects” on the horizon for next year, Young has one wish as a director: more romance. “I want to do many more rom-coms. I want to do a lot more romance. At the end of my life, I’d like to look back and be able to see the through line, and I think it continues to reveal itself,” she says. “So far in my career I’ve sailed across different genres, and I’m extremely motivated by asking myself, ‘Why do people like this genre?’ That motivates me to go try to fall in love with it. I’m just trying to understand love, and it takes a trillion forms. We’re specks in the universe in a nanosecond of geological time. There’s a simplicity I like — like a good poem that has to iterate itself over and over again to get to a truly beautiful form.” Clashing arrives as onscreen love stories are booming and having now made several of her own, Young believes that “in this digital age we live in, human connection and the intimacy of human relationships are actually kind of novel at this point. She adds, “As women, we escape into romanticism because there are men and women out there who are able to see you, proverbially, and connect with you at a very deep level — and I think that’s sometimes quite hard to find in the real world. You’re not going to get that from a phone or from the internet. At the end of the day, as a director, I’m seeking that level of intimacy with myself and with the relationships in my life, so I can relate to the audience on that level.” “As we continue to evolve as a species, these questions about love and what it means to be vulnerable in a relationship are incredibly important,” she continues. “Romance and desire are the most interesting things to explore, I think. So it’s not surprising to me at all that there’s a ravenous appetite for it.” Going forward, Young also finds great inspiration in “female characters who have a journey to go on.” She explains, “Women are these incredibly complex, raw gems that continue to reveal themselves the more you turn them. So I look for bravery in the characters, and if I can see that, then I can probably carry that torch over the finish line.” Though her sights are set on love, would the self-described “horror girly” return to the genre? Young is open to it but doesn’t want “to chase it.” “I want it to come to me,” she says. “I don’t know when or where yet, but when I get my horror fangs out, I can’t wait.” “I want to do many more rom-coms. I want to do a lot more romance.“ Everett *** Clashing Through the Snow is available on Prime Video. THR
